paragraphs.text: II. Against the Letter of Parmenian.
Book One.

On other occasions I have discussed many things against the Donatists, as far as the strength the Lord supplies allows, partly in writing and partly also in preaching. Now, however, a certain letter has come into our hands that Parmenian, formerly their bishop, wrote to Tyconius. Tyconius was a man endowed with a keen mind and rich eloquence, but a Donatist all the same, and Parmenian thought he was in error on the very point where Tyconius had been compelled to confess the truth. The brothers asked me, or rather commanded me, to reply here to this letter of Parmenian, chiefly because of certain testimonies from the Scriptures which he does not understand as they ought to be understood. For Tyconius, battered on every side by all the voices of the sacred pages, woke up and saw the church of God spread throughout the whole world, just as had been foreseen and foretold of it so long before through the hearts and mouths of the saints. Having seen this clearly, he undertook to demonstrate and maintain against his own people that no person's sin, however wicked and monstrous, can set aside the promises of God. Nor, he argued, can any impiety of any persons placed within the church bring it about that God's faithfulness is made void concerning the church that was to be spread to the ends of the earth, a faithfulness held fast in the promises to the fathers and now displayed. But while Tyconius argued this forcefully and at length, and stopped the mouths of his opponents with many great and clear testimonies of the holy Scriptures, he did not see what followed and ought to have been seen. Namely, the Christians in Africa who belong to the church spread throughout the world are those joined by communion not to these people, who are cut off from the communion and unity of that same world, but to the world itself. Parmenian and the other Donatists, however, saw that this followed. They preferred to adopt a most obstinate attitude against the most evident truth that Tyconius maintained, rather than concede it and be defeated by the African churches that rejoiced in communion with the unity Tyconius maintained, the unity from which they had separated themselves. At first Parmenian thought he should correct him, as it were, by letter; later, they report, Tyconius was even condemned by a council of theirs. So in this work we have decided to reply to the letter that Parmenian wrote to Tyconius, rebuking him for preaching a church spread throughout the whole world and warning him not to dare do so.

First, then, let us see what to make of his claim that the Gauls, the Spaniards, the Italians and their associates (by whom he of course means the whole world) are just like the African traditors through dealings in crimes and partnership in wrongdoing. Tyconius brings forward from the holy Scriptures so many and such weighty proofs, and Parmenian answers him without proofs and wants to be believed while proving nothing. He is evidently inviting Tyconius to imitate him, since he too believed certain fellow bishops of his on nothing but their word, against so many churches established across the whole breadth of all the lands. What could be found more reckless than such credulity? For he says that certain men who had served on an embassy came to those same provinces, most trustworthy witnesses, as he asserts. Then, by a second visit of "most holy priests of the Lord," as he calls them, the charges they make were published clearly, more fully and more truly. What a man, who thinks he ought to be believed rather than God! Tyconius brings forth the thunders of the divine testament, given in the promise to Abraham, the promise to Isaac and the promise to Jacob, whose God he declares himself to be, saying: "I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever." And this man sets against it the stories of his fellow priests. What was said to Abraham? "In your seed all nations will be blessed." What was said to Isaac? "And all the nations of the earth will be blessed in your seed, because Abraham your father heard my voice." What was said to Jacob? "I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; do not fear. For the land on which you are sleeping I will give to you and to your seed. And your seed will be like the sand of the earth, and it will spread out to the sea and to the south and to the north and to the east. And all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in you and in your seed." And so that they do not think this was said of the Jews, let the apostle explain what the seed of Abraham is, in which it was said that all nations would be blessed: "The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' which is Christ." So it was promised with such great authority and displayed with such great truth that all nations would receive blessing in Christ, and yet those who want to be called Christians contradict it. And what do they set against this? "Certain most trustworthy witnesses," he says, "who had served on an embassy, came to those same provinces; then, by a second visit of most holy priests of the Lord, it was published clearly, more fully and more truly." What, I ask you, what was published through these trustworthy witnesses, whom you want to be more trustworthy than God? That because of the African traditors the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, was not allowed to reach all nations, and withered where it had already reached? Go on, tell us now that your colleagues are to be believed rather than the testament of God. And while you say this, boast that you saved from the flames that very testament which you are trying to wipe out with your tongue.

But let each person choose what he likes. And if the smoke of earthly falsehood has any power against the lightnings of heaven, let him abandon heaven and vanish into the winds. For if Parmenian were not partial to his own see, he would choose to believe God's Scripture rather than his colleagues. For God says to Jacob: "I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you." It is certainly far more credible that these men had already been rejected by a just judgment and were therefore not admitted to communion in those regions where God was already fulfilling what he had promised our fathers. For that reason they spread such stories about God's holy priests, by whom they had not deserved to be received. With these false rumours they meant to stir up the weak minds of the congregations they had deceived, and to tear away from the peace of the whole world minds that were rashly credulous and ensnared by the pride of their party's name. What could be found more insane than this folly, or rather this madness? Among so many nations of the world God has already fulfilled in large part, and is still fulfilling, what he promised, until it reaches absolutely all of them; he is the one who said: "I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you." Yet these men now believe those who report that what God promised is not being fulfilled. They believe that the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, has therefore perished from the lands where the promise had already been fulfilled, and that God's promises have been made void, because they themselves were not admitted to communion with those among whom the world already held the promise fulfilled. And no one says to them: "God alone is true, but every man is a liar. You say these things from what is your own, for whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own. So you lie as men because you are angry as men." This is not said to them. Instead, they are even believed when they say that Christ has perished from the world, which he had already begun to possess. And those who believe this, while they shamelessly say "We are Christians," dare to say "We alone are."

Parmenian also says that the world is proved to have become an accomplice in the crimes of handing over and in other sacrileges by the following fact: although many such things were committed in the time of persecution, no separation of congregations took place afterwards in those provinces. As if it could not have happened that some wicked men remained hidden and were never accused in a way that would allow them to be condemned without any rashness, while others were exposed and condemned and, convicted on plain facts, stopped disturbing and dividing the churches! In that way some were not accused, certain uncertain charges were left to God for the sake of a certain peace, and others were so clearly exposed and proved that the men were condemned and no condemned man could deceive the people with feigned innocence. And so the bond of unity was in no way broken. Nor would this monstrous evil of cutting off have happened in Africa either, had not a faction of men inventing falsehoods prevailed over the true reasoning of those who proved their case.

Let those who wish read what Optatus, bishop of Milevis in the Catholic communion, of venerable memory, relates, and how many things he establishes and with what proofs. He writes about Lucilla, at that time an extremely wealthy and highly factious woman, whom the holy Caecilian, while still a deacon, had offended for the sake of church discipline. He writes about the other members of her faction, some of them thieves of the church's silver, others resentful at not having attained the episcopate, who harried Caecilian, preferred over them, with whatever plots they could. And he writes about the Numidian bishops, whom this faction had summoned to destroy Caecilian, so that he would be deposed and another bishop ordained for them. They came with Secundus of Tigisis, their primate at the time, and with others whose confessed crimes of handing over Secundus himself had pardoned, supposedly out of concern for peace, as the church records attest. Without any delay for a more careful inquiry, and allowing Caecilian no opportunity to reply, they declared him a traditor in his absence. So charges of handing over that were merely alleged were to count against him though he was absent, while they, who were present, had pardoned one another for crimes they had confessed. Thus they ordained another bishop against the man sitting in the see, with whom the whole Christian world was in communion, both in lands overseas and far away and in the weightier churches of Africa itself, which stood firmer against deceptions of this kind. They did this so that, in defence of their own deed, they could contradict the promises of God that all nations would be blessed in the seed of Abraham. They could then call even those parts of the world polluted by African traditors which had never heard Caecilian's name, or which at any rate had heard of his life as the life of an innocent man; and indeed these men never convicted him of any crime. Moreover, when the world says, "What you charge against your fellow citizens I could not investigate, and I ought not to condemn it without investigation," they bring forward against it the testimony of the apostle, who says: "Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them." For it was not enough for them to condemn so many great Christian peoples unheard; they must also dare to produce, against the apostle himself, his words but not his meaning. For if being with evildoers in the church is consenting to them, then the apostle himself consented to the false brothers among whom he testified that he was in danger. He also allowed some to preach the gospel even though they preached it not sincerely but out of envy and without love. But if consenting to evildoers is nothing other than approving and praising their evil deeds, then, by the apostle's example, the world would not be consenting to the crimes of the Africans even if it knew of them and tolerated them for the sake of the church's peace. And yet these men do not prove that the world knew of them, even if they had been able to prove that the charges were true.

In vain, therefore, does Parmenian say that traditors condemned in Africa were received into the fellowship of holiness by the provinces overseas. This is what we must not believe. Otherwise, with sacrilegious rashness, we would condemn the whole world, founded in the unity of Christ, on the strength of these men's false accusation, instead of loving it on the strength of God's true promise. For which is more to be believed: what God said, "In your seed all nations will be blessed," or what these men say, "In the seed of the African traditors all nations are cursed"? Is what iniquity has committed to count for more than what truth has promised? Why, then, do we not rather believe that those who were received into communion by the overseas provinces were innocent and could not be crushed by slanderers, which can be shown more plausibly by many proofs? Or at any rate, if they could not be convicted, then even if they were wicked they were believed innocent and received without any defilement to those who received them. And what of this? There are wicked brothers such as the apostle tolerated within the unity of the church, and such as the martyr Cyprian laments in his letter on the lapsed. Suppose that through brothers of this kind, even some placed among the judges, it had been brought about by some corruption that the traditors could not be excluded and convicted, and the Christian world were deceived by their feigned innocence. Even then it would in no way have lost its own innocence.

As for what he said about Hosius of Cordoba, once a Catholic bishop, they must be required to prove not only that he was what they say he was, but also that it was evident he was such to those with whom they claim he was in communion. Unless they prove this, it is pointless for them to say they knew what he was, since he could not harm those who did not know. And in separating themselves from those innocent people, these men cannot be innocent, because of the sacrilegious iniquity of the separation itself. For this is more credible, if indeed Hosius was condemned by the Spaniards and acquitted by the Gauls: the Spaniards may have been entrapped by false accusations and deceived by the clever fraud of plotters, and so pronounced sentence against an innocent man. Afterwards, peaceably and in Christian humility, they yielded to the judgment of their colleagues, to whom his innocence had been proved. They did so in order not to defend their earlier sentences with stubborn and passionate perversity and so rush, in the blindness of impiety, into the sacrilege of schism, which surpasses all crimes. That is what these wretched men have done, and though they have been divided and cut up so many times, they do not realize what they have done, even this late.

So they make it clear enough why they became incurable. They did not want to be forced to condemn their earlier sentences, which they had rashly pronounced against Caecilian in his absence, as they would have been if, out of regard for truth and peace, they had accepted the judgment overseas, where they were defeated by Caecilian in person. Yet they would have carried off a greater victory by overcoming human passion, at least after the judgment, than by overcoming a man in the judgment itself. For that victory is loftier, and richer in a loftier triumph, than one won not merely over a single defeated man but over a whole subjugated city, as Scripture says: "Better is he who conquers anger than he who takes a city." So they wanted to conquer a man while anger was conquering them. And since they could not conquer the man, they were overcome both by the man and by anger: by the man, because they were defeated in the judgment; by anger, because even in defeat they did not rest. With a most perverse heart they heard or read the apostle's statement: "For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor." If the apostle himself had understood these words with so perverse a mind, he would never have become a Christian or an apostle, nor would he as a preacher have built up the churches which he had once torn down as a persecutor. Nowhere, then, have these men revealed so openly why they refused to be corrected even when defeated as when they denounce the Spaniards for yielding to their colleagues' later examination and judgment after having pronounced their own sentences differently. For the one was done out of Christian gentleness just as surely as the other was done out of diabolical contentiousness. So it is no wonder that peace was preserved by the humility of the one and shattered by the arrogance of the other. They are therefore rightly paid back for what they did, for they taught such things to those who came after them. The Maximianists, too, refused to yield to the council of three hundred and ten of their colleagues, which judged innocent Primian, the man they themselves had first condemned. They refused for no other reason than this: with reckless obstinacy they set the apostle's statement before the unlearned and said, "For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor." For a hundred colleagues had torn Primian down, and therefore they refused to build him up again together with the three hundred. Thus, while pretending to take care not to build up a man they had torn down, they tore themselves down in another schism, by a greater sacrilege.

Yet if Parmenian were alive, he would not now dare to rebuke the Spaniards and call them transgressors for bending their sentence to their colleagues' sentence, for fear of offending his own colleagues. Many of them, after condemning Primian, corrected themselves for the better and went over to the council of the three hundred. They chose to go against their own over-hasty sentences rather than against the peace of unity, even within the party of Donatus. Above all, Parmenian would spare Praetextatus of Assuras and Felicianus of Musti. Though condemned by three hundred and ten of their fellow bishops, they returned out of zeal for concord to the very men who had condemned them. With the same zeal, their condemners received them for the sake of peace without any loss of their rank, and no one thought that those they had baptized outside, in schism, needed to be rebaptized. Or perhaps, since those who correct their sentences greatly displease Parmenian, and since he misunderstands the apostle and calls them transgressors, he would denounce these men for choosing to come back in rather than remain outside? Would he gather some like-minded associates and create Parmenianists as well, just as many fragments have already been broken off from that great fragment all over Africa? So it must be, so it must: those who have preferred the swelling of their own passion to the most holy bond of Catholic peace perish, cut and chopped into little pieces. For what Parmenian alleges is not so much to be feared as what he admits is to be noted.

He said that help was given to Caecilian through Hosius the Spaniard, so that the company of the holy and unblemished would be forced into communion with them, and that the unimpaired faith of God's servants resisted this impiety. In saying this, he admitted of his own accord that his own people had even gone to Constantine. By Constantine's decision the case was heard by bishops sitting as judges, presided over by Miltiades, bishop of the city of Rome. In that judgment, as the church records attest, these men were defeated and Caecilian was found innocent, and for that reason they accuse that same Miltiades of the crime of handing over. I ask when they learned this. If they learned it before the judgment, they ought not to have prejudiced their own case by beginning to plead it before such a judge and submitting to his judgment by order of the emperor, to whom they themselves had appealed. But if they claim to have learned that he was a traditor after the case had been argued and the sentence pronounced, are people so mad as to believe defeated litigants against the judges before whom they were defeated? And yet in all this they accuse, with great rashness to be sure, the Italians, the Gauls and the Spaniards. They leave aside the many other provinces and nations from which they have separated themselves by an abominable sacrilege, nations which the crimes of the Italians, Spaniards and Gauls certainly could not harm, even if the charges were true. For by now they accuse the other lands blindly, or rather madly, and are angry with them because, when there were two parties in Africa, one, they say, of traditors and the other of innocent men, those lands chose to join themselves to the traditors rather than to the innocent. This empty accusation is refuted very briefly and very truly as follows. When those lands heard that there were two parties in Africa, one of traditors and the other of innocent men, they believed that the innocent party was the one that had won its case before nearby church judges. Therefore those who did not know how these things had been done in Africa, but nevertheless believed what they ought in peace and piety to believe, always remained innocent; and separation from these innocent people could in no way be innocent.

Parmenian also admits that the bishops acting as judges and the parties from Africa, that is, Caecilian and the Donatists, met at the town of Arles. There he believed everything his own people said, though in defeat they could do nothing but complain about the judges. Nor does he deny that they came back to Constantine; and because they were defeated there too, in the final judgment, he accuses even Constantine of having been corrupted by favour. Having considered all this, let anyone who judges without partisanship choose whom to believe: the judges who pronounced the sentences, or the litigants against whom the sentences were pronounced and who refuse to end the dispute. And the world certainly believed the judges. Those who side with the Donatists and defend them, however, admit that they believe men who, whatever their case may have been, still could not win it in so many hearings overseas. And with credulous folly they accept those men's grumblings and charges against the judges. In this they call themselves innocent, because they are unwilling to believe rashly that those they see defeated were defeated by the truth. How much more innocent, then, are those who are unwilling to believe anything bad rashly about the judges themselves, about whom the losers are bound to complain! For it is not only one who has lost a good case who complains of an unjust, slow or careless judge. Even one who has been quite justly defeated grumbles against an innocent judge with the same blindness with which he went to law against an innocent opponent. So these people are wicked not because they are unwilling to believe something rashly about defeated men, but because in the frenzy of schism they have cut themselves off from those innocent people who, far more reasonably, are unwilling to believe any such thing about the judges themselves.

Let one of the most renowned churches in those regions in the name of Christ stand forth, one of those seven, and, if you please, Philadelphia above all, whose mystical name signifies brotherly love in Greek. Let us hear its voice, then, and let its wheat speak, not its chaff. Suppose it says to these men: 'What do you charge against me, brothers? What do you accuse me of? How far I lie from Africa in earthly distance, you know partly from your own knowledge and partly from hearsay. What was done there at that time by traitors, or by the accusers or condemners of traitors, or by the slanderers or oppressors of the innocent, I simply do not know. But our Lord, who bought the whole world at the price of his blood, whose holy purchase the prophet sang of so long before, saying: They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They looked and stared at me; they divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots, did not leave the spaces between you and us empty and bare of Christians. He filled them all with the sanctification of his name. In that very psalm of the passion it is declared not only at what price he bought, but also how much he bought. For a little later it says there: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight, for the kingdom is his, and he shall rule over the nations. I might perhaps have been obliged to judge your case at that time if I were your neighbour, or else so far away that no other Christians lived between us and you, marked with the same name and at peace in the same unity. But many families of nations lie between, bought together with me by his blood, who worship in his sight alongside me. The report about you has passed to me through them. Being near, they were able to examine your case. If that was not done, you neglected it, for if the others had neglected you, you would have come all the way to us. But if some judgment was given, forgive me: I do not dare rashly to believe you, the defeated party, and with the same rashness to condemn your judges. Something else moves me very greatly as well. If you had been innocent and oppressed, you would at least love us, your brothers, who have done you no harm. We are well aware that your case was committed to your neighbours by the proper law of the church, and they know before God how they judged. Yet you try to tear us apart with curses and to pursue us with bitter hatred, and you even try to rebaptize us, as if because of you Christ had lost his inheritance among us. What good can we think of that case of yours? By not hesitating in the least to condemn brothers so very far away on rash suspicions, you show how justly your neighbours condemned you. Why should I not believe that a neighbouring judge could rightly have condemned a man after giving him a hearing, when that same man does not hesitate to condemn me, his brother, so far absent and without a hearing? He charges me with this as the greatest crime: that, since I could not be present, I believed the judges before whom the case was brought rather than the defeated litigants. Had I not believed those judges rather than them, then even if the defeated party were innocent, I could not be innocent. For we cannot see human hearts, and so we would be entangled in a great offence if we failed to keep church discipline by refusing to believe the judges. The case could go no further than them, and it was through them that the report could reach us. You cut yourself off from these innocent people by an impious separation, and do you call yourself innocent? If you really were, then, seeing in the holy scriptures that the harvest of your Lord cannot be separated from the tares and the chaff before the final sorting and winnowing, you would choose to be strong in bearing with the wicked rather than impious in deserting the good.' How many churches throughout the world, far, far away, must we suppose speak in these words that I have put in the mouth of Philadelphia, and how very just their words are!

Parmenian even dares to complain that Constantine ordered them to be led to the field, that is, to execution. They had been defeated before church judges, they could not prove their claims before him either, and they were still being carried along by sacrilegious frenzy into cutting off pieces of the holy church. He accuses Constantine of giving this order as an act of savagery at the prompting of Hosius the Spaniard. As always, he condemns people unheard on the strength of his own suspicions. As if someone else might not believe, more humanely and more plausibly, that it was rather at the prompting of Hosius, as a bishop, that the emperor changed the sentence to a milder punishment, though the crime was a most monstrous one, namely the sacrilege of schism. For what do these men not suffer justly? They suffer by the most high judgment of God, who presides over all and warns them by such scourges to beware of eternal fire, and they suffer both as their crimes deserve and through the order of the powers. Let them first prove that they are not heretics or schismatics. Then and only then let them freely raise their voices about their undeserved punishments, and then and only then let them dare to call themselves martyrs for the truth when they suffer something of this kind. Otherwise, if whoever pays a penalty at the hands of the emperor or of judges sent by him is at once a martyr, then all the prisons are full of martyrs and all the chains of the courts drag martyrs along. In all the mines martyrs toil in misery, martyrs are deported to every island, and in all places of punishment martyrs are struck by the sword of justice. All who are driven to the beasts are martyrs, and so are all who are burned alive at the order of judges. But if, as the apostle says, there is no power except from God, and the minister of God is an avenger for wrath upon the one who does evil; he does not bear the sword in vain. Do you wish not to fear the power? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For when any good man suffers, praise comes to him from the power of the one who inflicts it. But let the bad man not blame the cruelty of the power for what he deservedly suffers for his wickedness.

And yet what do these men suffer that compares with what they do? It only seems otherwise because most people keep their heart not in their heart but in their eyes. If blood flows from mortal flesh, whoever sees it shudders. But if souls cut off and separated from the peace of Christ die in the sacrilege of heresy or schism, no one mourns, because no one sees it. Indeed, by force of custom that death is even laughed at, though it is more hideous and more grievous, and, to speak plainly, more truly death. Meanwhile the authors of so many deaths openly mock, and do not even deign to discuss the matter with us so that the truth might be made plain. They suffer some temporal trouble through the most certain and most proper order of the powers, while they themselves, with private bands of madmen, commit far worse things everywhere and every day, under no royal law and no church law. Yet they call us persecutors of bodies and do not call themselves murderers of souls, though in their private licence they do not spare bodies either. But because Christian gentleness punishes an eye torn out in a quarrel much more severely than a mind blinded in schism, they speak out and speak against us, yet they do not speak with us. Truth compels them to fall silent, but wickedness will not let them be quiet.

Or is it perhaps not right for the emperor, or those whom the emperor has sent, to judge in matters of religion? Why, then, did your envoys come to the emperor? Why did they make him judge of their case, when they did not mean to follow his judgment? But what is the point of saying this? Suppose they establish that it is not the emperor's business to decree anything against those who follow perverse ways in religion. If he does so anyway and punishes them, will they therefore be martyrs? In that case the same claim will be open to all heretics. By the hidden command of God, through the visible command of men, many very severe measures have been enacted to restrain them. Nor would the claim be open only to heretics, who are at least whitewashed in some fashion with the Christian name, but even to the pagans themselves. For they too are certainly impious through false religion, and recent laws have ordered their images to be overturned and smashed and their sacrifices to be forbidden on pain of death. If any of them is condemned for such a crime, then, is he to be considered a martyr because he paid the legal penalty for a superstition that he thought was true religion? Surely no Christian of any kind dares to say that. Therefore not everyone whom the emperor punishes over some question of religion becomes a martyr. Those who think so do not see where they are heading: to the claim that even the demons can lay claim to the glory of martyrs. For they suffer this persecution through Christian emperors: almost throughout the whole world their temples are overturned, their idols smashed and their sacrifices taken away, and those who honour them are punished if they are caught. If it is utterly insane to say this, then it is not suffering that proves righteousness; rather, righteousness makes suffering glorious. So the Lord did not say in general terms, 'Blessed are those who suffer persecution.' He did not want anyone to cast a fog over the ignorant in this matter, or to seek the praise of martyrs while being condemned as he deserved. Instead he added a great distinction by which piety may truly be told apart from sacrilege. For he said: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake. But those who have divided the church of Christ in no way suffer for righteousness' sake. With a pretended righteousness they try, as it were, to separate the church from its chaff before the time, and they assail its wheat with false accusations. Yet they themselves have rather been separated from it like the lightest chaff by the various gusts of rumour. 'But,' they say, 'we did not do this.' Let them see, then, that they must first clear themselves on this question. Only then may they dare, if they suffer any troubles or penalties from Christian emperors, either to lodge a complaint about them or to claim them as glory. On this matter, that is, on the question of the schism itself, what I said above would be enough even if I said nothing else.

Or perhaps they will say this: even if they are convicted of sacrilegious dissension, so that they are not martyrs if they suffer anything for that madness, still it ought not to fall to the power of emperors to restrain or punish such things. Here I ask what they mean. That such powers should take no notice of corrupt or false religion? But we have already said a great deal about the pagans, and about the demons themselves, and how they suffer persecution from emperors. Do they object to this too? Why, then, do they themselves overturn temples wherever they can, and never stop doing such things, or avenging them, through the frenzy of the Circumcellions? Is private violence more just than royal diligence? But I pass over these things. What I ask is this. The apostle lists the works of the flesh as plain to see: 'which are,' he says, 'fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, carousing and the like.' What do these men think? Do they hold that the crime of idolatry is justly punished by emperors? Or, if they will not grant even this, why do they admit that the force of the laws is justly brought to bear against sorcerers, yet refuse to admit it against heretics and impious dissensions, when apostolic authority counts these among the same fruits of iniquity? Or perhaps they do not allow these powers of human institution to concern themselves even with such things? Why, then, does he bear the sword, he who is called the minister of God, an avenger for wrath upon those who do evil? Unless perhaps, as some of them, very ignorant indeed, are accustomed to take it, this was said of church offices, so that the sword is to be understood as the spiritual punishment that excommunication carries out. But the most far-sighted apostle makes it clear enough what he is talking about in the passage that follows. For there he added: 'For this reason you also pay taxes,' and then went on: 'Pay to all what is due: tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue, honour to whom honour, fear to whom fear.' All that remains, then, is for them to use these arguments of theirs to forbid Christians to pay taxes. Yet when the Pharisees, whom these men imitate, thought such things, the Lord looked at a coin and answered them: 'Render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's.' These men, however, are disobedient and impious on both counts: they render neither Christian love to God nor human fear to kings. They are so blind and insane that, after they themselves have shut their own schismatics, the Maximianists, out of the basilicas through officials sent by Catholic emperors, and forced them to give way by the great force of orders and armed help, they find fault with the Catholic Church if Catholic princes order something of the kind done on its behalf. As for the Maximianists themselves, let them recall what they did before they were Maximianists, that is, while they were still held together in the one fellowship of the Donatists. Let them recall how savage and how bitter were the sufferings that the well-known Rogatus the Moor endured at their hands through the barbarian king Firmus, and let them keep silent. Let them not dare to complain if they suffer anything of this kind, either at the hands of the Primianists because of their own schism, or along with the Primianists because of the schism of the Donatists, not for holy religion but for sacrilegious animosity.

For perhaps they say that they have suffered worse things from Catholic emperors than they themselves inflicted on the Rogatists through barbarian kings, or on the Maximianists through the judges of Catholic emperors, or even than they inflict on whomever they can through the frenzy of the Circumcellions. As if the question were whether they suffer worse than they do, which I would not grant in any case. For many of their deeds, most savage and most cruel, can be counted, or rather are past counting. Even if they were fewer, or afflicted their victims less, they would certainly be worse for this very reason: they are not ordered by duly established powers but committed in lawless frenzy. The things they did against the Maximianists through judges of human institution are not so very many. Let them include in that category, if they like, what they did through the barbarian Firmus to persecute Rogatus the Moor, and let them count Firmus, though a most savage enemy of the Romans, among the lawful powers. But even these are not as many as the things committed every day, against all order of laws and powers, by the frenzied gangs of drunken young men over whom they set leaders. At first these men armed themselves only with clubs, but now they have begun to arm themselves with iron as well, and they roam and rage throughout Africa under the notorious name of Circumcellions. When their crimes are reported to them, they pretend not to know of such a class of men, or with the most shameless effrontery they assert, contrary to what everyone knows, that the Circumcellions have nothing at all to do with them. Yet they will not accept even this plea from the whole world, though the world says, far more plausibly and truly, that it does not know what was done in Africa, whether by the party of Donatus or against it. If Donatist bishops in Africa itself may either not know the deeds of the Donatist Circumcellions or say that these deeds have nothing to do with them, surely the world may say this.

But, as I had begun to say, the question now is not whether they suffer worse things than they do, but whether it is lawful to do anything of this kind against heretics and schismatics. If they say it is not lawful, why do they do it themselves? But if they admit that it is lawful, then suppose they could show, which they cannot in any way, that they suffer worse things from Catholic emperors than they themselves did to their own schismatics through the emperors' judges or through barbarian kings, or than they do to every class of men through the madness of the Circumcellions. Even so, this is nothing to wonder at, if princes have more power than the judges sent by princes, if Roman emperors have more power than barbarian kings, and if a robber deservedly suffers worse under the laws than he himself commits against the laws. So it is right that the masters of the Circumcellions should suffer worse things under just enactments than the Circumcellions commit. And yet so great is Christian gentleness that their crimes incomparably exceed their punishments. But look: three hundred and ten Donatist bishops condemned the Maximianists in their council, and the Maximianists, in their stubborn perversity, refused to give up the basilicas. The judges were approached, and the council's decision was entered in the proconsular records. Then it was ordered that those condemned by so large a number of bishops should give up the places. Those who readily gave way did not suffer much; but who does not know how those who tried to resist were afflicted? And yet, if the savagery of the resisters had been so great as to reach the point of outrages against the judges, would they not have suffered far harsher things under Roman law? So it was then too. After the conclusion of the case in which these men cut themselves off from the Catholic Church, steps were duly taken to stop them holding the basilicas. But they held them by resisting imperial orders, and resisted in such a way that the notorious violence of the Circumcellions prevailed. On top of this, they harassed with most turbulent and savage riots those whom the emperor had sent through Africa with gifts for the church. And so laws were issued against them which did not allow them to keep even those basilicas that did not belong to the unity, but had been built by those who had separated and were already established in their schism. In this the royal power was by now avenging its own wrongs. For what can the enemies of justice justly possess?

Nor is anyone found to have issued anything in their favour except Julian the Apostate, who greatly disliked Christian peace and unity, since he disliked the very religion from which he had impiously fallen away. These Donatists petitioned him in such terms, as the records of the judges before whom they presented what they had obtained bear witness, that some who consented out of fear to the worship of idols perhaps did less than these men did in praising him so frenziedly. For they said that with him justice alone had a place. What else, then, are they found to have said, except either that Christian holiness, which had no place with him, is not justice, or that the honouring of demons, which had first place with him, is justice? But who does not know how severe were the laws that other emperors issued against them? Among these is one general law against all who wish to be called Christians but are not in communion with the Catholic Church, gathering instead in their own separate conventicles. It provides that both the one who ordains a cleric and the cleric ordained be fined ten pounds of gold, and that the very place where the impious separation assembles be confiscated to the treasury. There are other general decrees as well, which take away from them the right to make wills, or to give anything by gift, or to receive anything by gift or by will. For in one case a nobleman petitioned the emperors because his sister, who had belonged to the party of Donatus, had at her death left a great deal to various people of her communion, and especially to a certain Augustine, one of their bishops. Under that general law it was ordered that everything be restored to the brother. There mention was also made of the Circumcellions, setting out what kind of help and support should be used to drive them off if they resisted violently in their usual way. For they are so well known, and have proved themselves in so many battles, that neither the man petitioning the emperor nor the emperor could keep silent about them.

Such is the case: they are condemned in this way by both divine and human laws. Yet so great is Christian gentleness that they not only keep the basilicas they built after they had cut themselves off, but have not even returned to the unity all those that the unity held from the beginning. They themselves urgently drove the Maximianists out of basilicas belonging to the party of Donatus through judges sent by Catholic emperors. Yet they are not driven out of many places that Catholic unity formerly held, not even by the laws of those same Catholic emperors. Finally, if anything has perhaps at some time been done against them too harshly, so as to go beyond Christian mildness, it displeases all the wheat of the Lord's harvest, that is, the Christians who are praiseworthy in Christ and who grow in the Catholic Church throughout the world, bearing fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold or thirtyfold.

So let them accuse, as fully as they like and together with us, the tares or the chaff in the Catholic crop; but let them not refuse to bear with them, most patiently, together with us. For he who did not want the tares rooted up before the time and separated from the wheat they were mixed with said, "Let both grow until the harvest." And when he unfolded the meaning of this same parable to his disciples at their request, he did not say, "The field is Africa"; he said, "The field is this world." Across the whole world, then, this crop has been sown; across the whole world the tares have been sown over it; across the whole world both are growing until the harvest. Was Donatus, then, the chief of the reapers? Or had the time of harvest come at the moment when these people separated themselves from the whole world, when the same Lord, so that no one would be free to interpret it as he pleased, said quite plainly, "The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are the angels"? Such reapers cannot make mistakes: they will neither gather wheat as tares nor store up tares as wheat. But these people, by fleeing from others as though from tares, have shown that they themselves are the tares. In the most manifest sacrilege they preach against the Lord's own judgment: where he says, "Let both grow until the harvest," they maintain that throughout so great a field, that is, the whole world, only the tares have grown, while the wheat has dwindled and remains in Africa alone. In this they do sacrilegious injury to Christ, our King and Prince. For it is written: "In a multitude of people is the king's glory, but in the dwindling of the people is the prince's ruin." But now, I think, it is time to look carefully at the very testimonies of Scripture by which, through their bad interpretation, they deceive the unlearned, and to explain them, as far as the Lord grants, according to the understanding of Catholic truth.
BOOK TWO.

What force, after all, except blindness and vanity of mind drives men to throw something with their eyes shut, as the saying goes, as though at another, when it comes straight back on the thrower and strikes him with a rebounding blow, while the man he wanted to wound is left untouched? Yet this is what these Donatists do with nearly all the testimonies of the Scriptures. When they think they are bringing them forward against us, they seem instead to be reminding us what sort of people Scripture itself proves them to be. Parmenian thinks that this text either supports him or tells against us: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put light for darkness and darkness for light, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter." But what else does it do? O most foolish blindness! For what is so good and so pleasant as brothers dwelling in unity? Yet those who have separated themselves from all their brothers call this evil and count it bitter. They did this because they would neither refrain from raising their empty suspicions, not to say their factious slanders, nor bear patiently with them once they had raised them. If they hated the real chaff and were not chaff themselves, they would not cut themselves off because of it from the Lord's wheat, which is sown and growing through the whole field, that is, this world.

So let them cry out as loudly as they can: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil." We answer, "This is true," and we add something else: "Woe to those who have lost their endurance," since they put light for darkness and darkness for light. For what is brighter than the promises of God? In our own times he has shown what he foretold thousands of years ago, that all nations would receive a blessing in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ. And what is darker than the presumptions of men who say that the Christian name has perished from so many nations throughout the world and has survived in Africa alone? They say this because of crimes of traditors that were rashly alleged and never proved, crimes which, even if they were true, would never stop God from fulfilling what he promised. This presumption of theirs they call light, while they strive to cover God's promises with the darkness of lies, even though those promises are already lit up by the very outcome of events. On top of that, they shout their own deeds at us, saying: "Woe to those who put light for darkness and darkness for light." Was Optatus light, then, while all Africa called him darkness? Or did all Africa rather see that he was darkness, while these men called him light, these men who supposedly do not put light for darkness and darkness for light? "But Optatus," they say, "displeased all the good men in our communion." So you did not call him light, and yet you were in communion with him. Choose, then, which you prefer. The first possibility is that darkness does no harm to light within one communion, and that it is enough for the light to disapprove of the darkness and, if it cannot drive it out, to tolerate it for the sake of unity. In that case there was no reason for you to cut yourselves off, by the dark sacrilege of schism, from innocent brothers to whom you certainly could not point out the wicked, even if you claim that you knew who they were. The other possibility is that it is not enough for light to disapprove of the darkness it cannot drive out, that is, it is not enough for the good to disapprove of the wicked whom they can neither exclude nor correct. In that case, Optatus alone, who was utterly notorious and utterly open in Africa alone, defiled the party of Donatus far more easily than any African traditor defiled so many nations throughout the world. Such a traditor was at any rate unknown to them, even if I do not say that he was accused of false crimes, though this is something they most shamelessly deny.

So by receiving the Scriptures with a perverse heart they make them harm not us but themselves. They think that "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil" was written so that the wheat would not tolerate the chaff among it until the time of winnowing. As a result, while they misunderstand "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil," the words "Woe to those who have lost their endurance" are fulfilled in them. Suppose they understood that this was said against those who think that evil is good and so commit evil deeds, or against those who consent to such people by praising and approving them. Scripture mentions both kinds together in one place, saying: "For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who does wrong is blessed." Then they would understand rightly, and they would not be troubled when wicked men are found among themselves as well. As it is, they tolerate for the sake of Donatus' party those whom they ought to have tolerated for the sake of Christ's unity. Through this obstinate animosity of theirs the wretched men are forced to put up with those they know within their own schism, while accusing those they do not know throughout the world. Here, then, is the peacemaker. He corrects by rebuke what he can. What he cannot correct he excludes, while keeping the bond of peace. What he cannot exclude while keeping the bond of peace he disapproves of fairly and bears with firmly. Such a man is entirely free from the curse in which Scripture says: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put light for darkness and darkness for light, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter." He is completely secure from it and wholly untouched by it.

Again, with their usual blindness, they throw something similar at us. "Scripture says of you," they say, "'He who judges the just unjust and the unjust just is abominable before God.'" Why does this curse not fall instead on those who dared to condemn the whole Christian world unheard? In that world, among so vast a number of people, there were and are, beyond any doubt, people innocent of the crimes they allege. In this way they have judged what is just to be unjust and what is unjust to be just. Meanwhile they kept Optatus the Gildonian, who for ten years made all Africa groan, in their communion and honored him as a bishop and colleague. Or if they disapproved of him in their hearts but tolerated him for the sake of peace, let them learn that no wicked people can stain the patience of a peacemaker who does not consent to evil. Then let them see in what ruin they lie, who fail to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace with the whole world because of the crimes of Africans, whether those crimes are false or true, for that is not the question now. If they said, "We do not know whether there are good Christians among so many nations in the lands overseas," they would be speaking most shamelessly. For God bears witness to his wheat. He sowed it through the whole field and foretold that it would grow until the harvest, even though the devil would sow tares over it. So even if we do not know those people very well, we still know that they exist, because we hold with the most certain faith that God could not have lied. If it would be sacrilegious shamelessness for them to say, "We do not know whether there are good Christians in the rest of the world," let them see with what madness they dare to say, as they do not hesitate to say every day, "We know that there are no Christians there." It is certainly one thing to say, "We do not know whether they exist," and another to say, "We know that they do not exist." Both are faithless and impious. But if a man who says, "I do not know whether God spoke the truth," is to be detested, what is a man who says, "I know that God did not speak the truth"?

Surely I should offend none of them if I put God before Donatus. However much they love Donatus, they fear God more. In any case, however much they love Donatus, we know that God alone is true and every man is a liar. Christ is God over all, blessed forever, and he said with perfect truth of himself, "I am the truth." When his servants asked him whether he wanted them to go and gather up the tares, he said, "Let both grow until the harvest." Donatus, however, says that the tares have indeed grown but the wheat has dwindled. Let them choose whom to believe. Christ, that is, the Truth, says, "The field is this world." Donatus, however, says that Africa alone has remained God's field. Let them choose whom to believe. Christ, that is, the Truth, says, "At harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather the tares first," and he explains this by saying, "The harvest is the end of the age." Donatus, however, says that the tares were separated from the wheat before the harvest when his party cut itself off. Let them choose whom to believe. Christ, that is, the Truth, says, "The reapers are angels." Donatus, however, says that before the harvest he and his colleagues did what Christ said the angels would do at the harvest. Let them choose whom to believe. They certainly call themselves Christians, so we set Christ and Donatus before them. If they give their words to Christ but their heart to Donatus, let them consider what they are. I am sparing them. I do not attack them or exaggerate; I would rather keep my grief in than let it out. But if they say that they give their heart to Christ, then let them believe Christ. He says that throughout the whole world both the children of the kingdom and the children of the evil one are growing. Let them not believe Donatus, who says that throughout the world only the children of the evil one have grown, while the good children have dwindled until only Africa is left. If they believe Christ, then we no longer say "Let them be at peace with the churches of the whole world," but "Let them be at peace with the gospel itself." They keep boasting that they saved the gospel from the fire, but this is a lie, since their deeds do not prove it.

Now what is the point of the passage from the prophet Isaiah that the same Parmenian thought he should throw at us? "Is the hand of the Lord not strong enough to save, or has he made his ear dull, so that he cannot hear? No, your offenses have divided you from God, and because of your sins he has turned his face away from you so as not to show mercy. For your hands are defiled with blood and your fingers with sins. Your lips have spoken iniquity, and your tongue plots injustice. No one speaks what is just, and there is no true judgment. They trust in empty things and speak what is empty, for they conceive pain and give birth to iniquity. They have hatched the eggs of asps and they weave the spider's web. Whoever was going to eat those eggs crushed one and found it rotten, with a basilisk inside it. Their web will not serve for clothing, and they will not cover themselves with their works. For their works are works of iniquity, and their feet run to wickedness, swift to shed blood, and their thoughts are the thoughts of fools. Ruin and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace." Those whom Scripture describes in this passage do no harm to the good, wherever they are, even when they are among the good. In the same way the chaff does no harm to the wheat until the Lord of the threshing floor comes with his winnowing fan in his hand. He will clean his threshing floor, store the wheat in the granary, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. In the same way, too, so great a multitude of the wicked did no harm to the good, as we learn from the prophet Ezekiel. He means those who sighed and mourned over the crimes of the people that were being committed among them. Because they could not correct the wicked, and ought not in any way to separate themselves from the unity of God's people, they were found worthy to be marked as a reward for their wholly innocent forbearance, and to be delivered when those lost men were laid waste and destroyed. But why do the people who throw these things at Catholics not look at themselves? Their bands, like frenzied herds, rush here and there armed with swords and clubs. They commit slaughter as often as they can, and even in such savagery they are never satisfied. Women roam with them day and night, mixed in among them everywhere, against the order of things divine and human. At the tombs of their dead such drunkenness boils over that it breeds in them a daily madness, not only for attacking others but even for throwing themselves to their deaths. Do their feet not run to wickedness, and are they not swift to shed blood? Has judgment not departed from these men, who even claim for themselves the most unjust liberties of a lawless power? Does darkness not come upon them while they wait for light in a false martyrdom? Do they not walk in the middle of the night even by day, since the apostle says, "Those who get drunk are drunk at night"? Do they not stumble at noon as if it were midnight? This is indeed true of all heretics. They cannot see a thing that is perfectly plain and set in the light of all nations. Whatever they do outside its unity, however great the skill and care with which it seems to be done, is of as little use to them against the wrath of God as spiders' webs are against the cold.

What do they cite from this prophetic chapter, then, that cannot be turned back on themselves? Perhaps only the asps' eggs, which the man who drafted the sentence of the plenary council of three hundred and ten made so much of when they assembled from all the provinces of Africa. Surely, if Parmenian were alive now, he would not say this, nor would he cite against us from the prophet Isaiah, "They have hatched the eggs of asps." For he would look at Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuras, who have been joined to his own college. These men were among the condemned, yet they received them back as though they were blameless, supposedly for the good of peace, though not the peace of Christ but the peace of Donatus. These men were both asps' eggs and hatched ones. For that is how the three hundred and ten of the plenary council describe them with their truthful mouth, as their acts testify, which were also entered in the proconsular records. These are certainly the words of their council: "For although the hollow of a poisoned womb long concealed the harmful offspring of viperous seed, and the moist clots of conceived crime were slowly warmed by a sluggish heat into the limbs of asps, yet the venom once conceived could not be hidden under a fading shelter. For, though late, the crime-laden womb of their desires has brought forth its public wickedness and its parricide." These asps' eggs had already hatched, and they had already been cast out of their communion, horrid and foul-smelling, along with their venomous brood. But inside was Optatus the basilisk, who could recall even the expelled asps by a kind of royal nod, the kind by which the basilisk is said to rule over the serpents. Or if these things do no harm for the sake of peace, why do they throw at Catholics charges they could not prove against them, when they themselves have received back men they condemned with their own mouth? If these things do no harm for the sake of peace, they certainly do harm for the sake of the peace of Donatus, which they greatly favor to the injury of the peace of Christ. For this sacrilege, whatever bodily troubles they suffer are God's warning to beware of eternal damnation. For they truly shed blood, not only bodily through the frenzy of the Circumcellions but also spiritually, since they try to rebaptize the whole world if they can. Or suppose that only a man who wounds mortal flesh, or kills by wounding it, sheds blood, while a man who kills souls he has led astray through the sacrilege of schism does not. Why, then, did they say such things in the same sentence of their plenary council against their own schismatics, the Maximianists: "Their feet are swift to shed blood"? It is established that the Maximianists killed no one bodily and wounded no one. On the contrary, they suffered much at the hands of these men when they were driven out of their basilicas by the judicial authorities. Before the Maximianists separated, while they were all still together in one body, these men had done many such things to many others who had made earlier schisms from the party of Donatus. For which of their own schismatics have they ever spared? Yet they most shamelessly want to be spared by the world, from which they themselves are schismatics. If schisms are to be punished in this way at all, it is only that one true unity which punishes them with perfect justice.

Then there is the text that is written: "As the ruler of the people is, so are his ministers, and as the governor of the city is, so are its inhabitants." If they understood what this refers to, they would neither throw it at us nor puff themselves up with empty boasting. Human hope is safe and rightly secure in God alone, and we do not want it placed in men, since we remember that it is written: "Cursed is he who puts his hope in man." For this reason we do not understand the ruler of the people and the governor of the city in this passage to mean the bishop. This is not because we cannot see countless holy bishops in the Catholic Church. It is so that, as I said, no one's hope may be placed in a man. Otherwise, if someone happens to live in a city where there is no good bishop, he might think he can become wicked with impunity. He would take this scripture for his defense, understanding it as perversely as these men do, and say that he cannot be good because "as the ruler of the people is, so are his ministers, and as the governor of the city is, so are its inhabitants." For the mouth of the Truth contradicts this error when he says: "Do what they say, but do not do what they do. For they say and do not do." Some congregations have bishops of this kind, who speak good things from the chair of Moses but do not do what they say because of their own pestilence. If those congregations do the good things the bishops say and do not do the evil things they do, as the Lord commanded, does this not show clearly enough that the ruler of the people and the governor of the city are not to be understood as these men understand them? There can be good peoples even where there are bad bishops, just as there could be a bad people where Moses was a good ruler and governor. For they go astray over the words of the holy Scriptures and, as the apostle says, "understand neither what they are saying nor the things about which they make assertions." Because of their perverse understanding, they themselves are the ones who end up in great difficulties when someone says to them: "Then as Optatus was, so was the people of Thamugadi. And if, as you say, communion in the sacraments contaminates even those who disapprove of evil deeds, including those they tolerate for the sake of unity, then all of you are like them too. For you were in communion both with that colleague of yours and with that people, when all Africa, groaning openly, declared him to be Gildo's henchman." I name him often for this reason: he was so notorious that wherever his name is mentioned, no one answers that he does not know him.

For let them look back and remember how many men like him they have among them, whose wickedness is equal but whose notoriety is not. Let them at last arrive at the true meaning of these words, and understand that the one ruler of the people is our Lord Jesus Christ, whose ministers are good. He is also the governor of that city, Jerusalem, which is our eternal mother in heaven. Its inhabitants are in keeping with the dignity of this governor, not by being his equals but in their own measure, since it has been said: "You shall be holy, for I too am holy." This means according to a kind of likeness to his image, into which we are being transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord, through the gift of him who makes us conformed to the image of his Son. The other people, the wicked one, also has a ruler, the devil, who is the governor of that city which is mystically called Babylon. For the apostle Paul calls the devil and his angels the rulers and governors of this darkness, that is, of sinners. His ministers are like him, because they disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness, just as he disguises himself as an angel of light. Its inhabitants match their most wicked governor by doing deeds like his. But these peoples and cities will be openly separated when this harvest has been winnowed. Until that happens, the love that unites the grain bears all things, so that the grains do not flee the chaff too hastily and so impiously separate themselves from their fellow grains.

What bearing on the case does it have now, then, when they throw at us what the Lord says through Isaiah about wicked sacrificers? "The criminal who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog, he who offers fine flour is like one who offers swine's blood, and he who offers incense as a memorial is like a blasphemer." All these words apply much more fittingly to those who have set up the altar of their schism against the church of God, which is spread, as was promised, through the whole world. That sacrilege entangles them all. Anyone anywhere who offers sacrifice with such a heart or such deeds that he deserves to hear these words brings ruin on himself. He does not bring it on those good people who, as the prophet Ezekiel says, sigh and mourn over the sins and iniquities committed among them, even though they do not separate themselves bodily, for the Lord rewards each one according to his heart. In earlier times wicked priests did no harm either to good colleagues such as Zechariah, or to good people of the laity such as Nathanael, in whom there was no guile. How much less, then, does a wicked bishop within Christian unity harm either good fellow bishops or good laypeople, now that we have that priest forever after the order of Melchizedek! He is our high priest, seated at the right hand of the Father and interceding for us, who was handed over for our offenses and rose again for our justification. So the saying "The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked," which is perfectly true, does not harm the good either, but only the wicked who make the offering. For he did not say, "The Most High does not approve the gifts of those who tolerate the wicked for the sake of peace." Besides, these men could not even prove the charges they made at the time when they created their schism. Had they proved them, the inheritance of Christ spread through the whole world would have excluded those others and kept these men in Catholic communion.

“The sacrifices of the wicked,” he says, “are an abomination to the Lord, for they offer them unjustly.” It has already been answered above that Christ is not unjust, who offered himself for us and is our mediator in heaven. While he governs his church, the wicked will not harm the good, whether those wicked are unknown or are tolerated for the sake of peace, until he himself comes and, sending the reapers ahead, separates the tares from the harvest, and with the winnowing fan the chaff from the wheat. And yet these men, as must often be said, have brought false charges. Even if the charges were true, they would do no harm to the charity of the good, which bears all things for the sake of unity within unity, if perhaps those things, even when known, could not be proved to the church's judges. The sacrifices of the wicked, then, will harm those very people who offer them wickedly. For one and the same sacrifice, because of the name of God which is invoked there and is always holy, becomes for each person according to the heart with which he has come to receive it. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself. He does not say “upon others” but “upon himself.” So whoever eats and drinks worthily eats and drinks grace for himself. Let those men consider, then, whether they eat worthily. Among so many parents and children, husbands and wives, and above all among so many heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ spread throughout the whole world, they have caused division by a wicked schism. Yet if they were good and were truly rebuking the wicked, they could certainly have tolerated fruitfully for the peace of Christ what they now tolerate to their ruin for the party of Donatus.

“In Exodus,” he says, “it is written: Let the priests who come near to the Lord God be sanctified, lest the Lord perhaps forsake them. And again: When the ministers come near to the holy altar, let them not bring sin upon themselves, lest they die. And this in Leviticus: A man who has a blemish or defect shall not come near to offer gifts to God.” It is good that they put forward these testimonies from the old books. Let them tell me, then, which holy man, whether he was placed among the priests or among the people, had his spiritual salvation harmed by a wicked or blemished priest. Where Moses and Aaron were, there were sacrilegious murmurers, whom God kept threatening to destroy from before his face. Where Caiaphas and others like him were, there was Zechariah, there was Simeon, and other good men. Where Saul was, there was David. Where Jeremiah, Isaiah, Daniel and Ezekiel were, there were wicked priests and wicked peoples. But each one bore his own burden.

I pass over the wicked pride of claiming that none of their colleagues, and not they themselves, has any blemish and defect, not of the limbs but, what is worse, of character. When we begin to press them on this, they answer that it matters what kind of blemish and what kind of defect it is, as if Scripture had made such a distinction when it says: A man who has a blemish or defect shall not come near to offer gifts to God. I will not even ask about Optatus. Did Parmenian himself, or Donatus himself, have no blemish and no defect? But these men are so blinded by love of men, and with an unchaste heart they so readily make the adulterers of their mind equal to the one lawful husband, that they contend that what could be said of the Lord Jesus Christ alone was fulfilled in Donatus too. Who will give my eyes a fountain of tears? What groan from a smitten breast could fit such a crime? But meanwhile let them consider whether at least Optatus had some blemish or some defect. They are not so blind as to answer that his life too was wholly unblemished and free of every defect. Why, then, did he come near to offer gifts to God, and why did the others, with joined hands, receive from him what a blemished and defective man had offered? Let them consider among the rest of their people whether drunkenness is no blemish; but first let them read with what criminals the apostle Paul ranked drunkards. And let them consider whether greed is no blemish, which the same apostle detests so much that he likens it to the service of idols.

Those who think most rightly understand that any human being cannot be without some fault as long as the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, even though, in view of our fellowship in human society, it might not absurdly be said that he lives most justly. They understand both that “whoever is born of God does not sin” and that “if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” For although we do not sin insofar as we are born of God, there is still in us what we are from Adam, since death has not yet been swallowed up in victory. That is promised in the resurrection of bodies, so that we who are already sons of God by faith may be blessed, unblemished and incorrupt in every way; but in visible form it has not yet appeared what we shall be. For we have been saved not yet in reality but in hope. Hope that is seen is not hope, for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. As long as we wait with patience for the redemption of our body, let us not dare to say that we lack every fault, lest that very pride be the most monstrous fault. And let us at last wake up and see that the priests of that time, when bodily defects were shunned, prefigured him who, though he was God, became man for our sake, alone truly the unblemished lamb and the priest without defect. That is why the priest alone used to enter the holy of holies while the people stood outside, just as now that priest has entered the secret places of heaven after the resurrection, to intercede for us at the right hand of the Father, while the people whose priest he is still groan outside. For in the church the people are inside with the bishop; they pray with him and, as if signing their names to his words, respond “Amen.” So in that time, when priests were required to be without any blemish and without any defect of body, since such perfection could not be required of their souls, he alone was prefigured. It was not these proud and impious men, who are not jealous for the bridegroom when the soul commits fornication, but dare to present themselves to souls in the bridegroom's place.

“In the Gospel,” he says, “it is written: God will not hear sinners; but if anyone worships the Lord and does his will, him he will hear.” Here too the reply is straightforward. If two people pray at the same time, one a sinner and the other someone who worships the Lord and does his will, he surely hears the one and does not hear the other. What, then, does this testimony mean, or how do they think it can be brought forward in their favour? By these very words the good are made most secure among the wicked, and there is no reason for a bodily separation that would cut people off by a wicked schism, through spiritual discord, even from the good. After all, the wicked among the good can go unheard because of their unbelief, and the good among the wicked can be heard because of their faith. For God, who searches the heart, does not err, as if he might hear or reject one person in place of another. Or do they say this so that we will understand that a wicked bishop is not heard when he prays for the people? Even if that were so, the people, if they are good and faithful, ought not to be anxious on that account. For they are made secure by the scripture which says: Brothers, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; and if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins. Let them hear with what truthful and devout humility this was said, if they have ears to hear with. John had said: I have written these things to you so that you may not sin. Suppose he had gone on to say: “And if anyone sins, you have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for your sins.” Then he would have seemed to set himself apart from sinners, as though he no longer needed the propitiation that comes through the mediator who sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us. That would certainly have been said not only proudly but also falsely. And suppose he had said: “I have written these things to you so that you may not sin; and if anyone sins, you have me as mediator with the Father; I make entreaty for your sins.” This is how Parmenian, in one passage, set up the bishop as a mediator between the people and God. Who among good and faithful Christians would have put up with John, and who would have regarded him as an apostle of Christ rather than as an antichrist? And yet these broken cisterns put up with the smoky pride of these men and cannot hold the Holy Spirit. So they do not keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, nor are they secure in all their prayers in the one mediator.

All Christians commend one another in their prayers. But he for whom no one intercedes, while he himself intercedes for all, is the one true mediator. Because he was prefigured in the priest of the Old Testament as his type, no one is found there either to have prayed for the priest. The apostle Paul was a principal member under the head, yet he was still a member of the body of Christ. He knew that the greatest and truest priest had entered for us, not in figure behind the veil into the holy of holies, but in truth made plain and fulfilled into the inner places of heaven, to a holiness not imaginary but eternal. So he too commends himself to the prayers of the church, and does not make himself a mediator between the people and God. In this way all the members of Christ's body pray for one another, since the members care for one another: if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it. Thus the prayer of all the members for one another while they still labour on earth will rise to the head, which has gone before into heaven and in which is the propitiation for our sins.
