For if Paul were a mediator, then surely his fellow apostles would be too, and so there would be many mediators, and Paul's own reasoning would not hold when he said: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. In him we too are one, if we keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. We must not desert the good because of the wicked, but bear with the wicked for the sake of the good. Otherwise, in trying to defend our rash presumption in abandoning people we do not know, we may be driven to the greater crime of condemning people unheard.

What of the fact that the Scriptures also tell of the prophet Balaam? He was not of the people of Israel but a foreigner, hired by an enemy to curse the people of God, and the Lord turned him to blessing. We hear and read all his words of blessing, and although he wished for something else, the words of his prayer are good and are heard by the Lord on the people's behalf. So it is no wonder that the good words spoken in prayers on the people's behalf are heard even when wicked bishops speak them. They are heard not because of the perversity of those set over the people, but because of the devotion of the peoples. Moreover, what is written in the Gospel, God does not hear a sinner; but if anyone worships the Lord and does his will, him he hears, was not said by the Lord. It was said by the man who indeed had the eyes of his body already restored, but whose eyes of the heart were not yet open, and so he still thought the Lord himself was a prophet. Afterwards, when he had come to know him as the Son of God, he worshipped him on his knees. The Lord himself, when a tax collector and a Pharisee prayed in the same temple, says that the sinner who confessed his sins was justified rather than the Pharisee who boasted of his merits, whom these men resemble. Once justified, the tax collector ceased to be a sinner. Yet it was as a sinner that he prayed to be justified and confessed his sins, and when he was heard he was justified, so that he ceased to be a sinner. So he would not have ceased to be a sinner unless he had first been heard as a sinner. The truth therefore bears witness, not that every sinner is heard, but that not every sinner goes unheard.

They also cite against us what is said in the Psalms: But to the sinner God says: Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth? You have hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you threw in your lot with adulterers. You sat and spoke against your brother, and against your mother's son you laid a stumbling block. But let them at last open the ears of their heart and stop understanding neither what they say nor the things they assert. They notice what is said to the sinner, Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth?, but they do not understand why it was said. It was said so that the sinner may know that the words of God he utters with his mouth are of no benefit to him if he does not himself do what he says. Yet those words benefit others, who hear even through the wicked and do what the Lord commands. The Lord himself teaches this in the Gospel, saying of the Pharisees: They sit on Moses' seat. Do what they say, but do not do what they do. For they say and do not do.

Would that they were willing to look at themselves in these words they have cited from the psalm, as in a mirror! There they would see how they cast God's words behind them, since they proclaim peace to the peoples and do not love peace. They would see how they hate discipline, since they dare to condemn the world unheard. In accordance with the discipline of divine mercy they suffer temporal troubles as they deserve, indeed far less than they deserve for the audacity of such madness, and yet they do not confess that their sins are being punished but boast that their merits are being crowned. I do not, of course, say that they ran with a thief, since a robber is worse than a thief, and that is what Optatus was loudly declared to be on every side. Or do they perhaps not throw in their lot with adulterers, when they shamefully let drunken flocks of their nuns roam about day and night mixed with drunken flocks of circumcellions? Or do they not sit and speak against their brothers? On account of certain men they could not convict, they contend that there are no Christians in the inheritance of Christ spread throughout the whole world. In this way they lay a most pernicious stumbling block against their mother's son, that is, one who is still a little child in faith and must be nourished with the milk of the sacraments. Not yet knowing how to follow God the Father, he weakly follows a man, and, lured by a feigned and shadowy appearance of truth, he is torn away from the fabric of unity by a cruel rending. But suppose those in that same party who do no evil are displeased by the evil deeds of the others, and believe that the crimes of others, committed in their midst while they groan and mourn over them, do not harm them. Then why do they tolerate to their ruin, in the common sacrilege of schism, what they could have tolerated fruitfully in the wholeness of unity? If, taught by the facts themselves, they at last wake up, they can say that the evils of individuals do not harm the rest, who neither do nor approve such things. But the sacrilege of schism is not the evil of individuals; it belongs to all who are not in communion with catholic unity. Of this they can very easily be convinced, even if they would admit it only with great difficulty. The very reason why the crimes of some do not belong to others in their communion is the reason why schism is the crime of all. When they say that among their own people they cannot be defiled by the crimes of others, they must at the same time admit that they had no reason to depart from unity, where the crimes of others could not defile them. Therefore they are all bound together alike by the most manifest crime of schism, as by a single deadly chain.

“But Jeremiah prophesied.” What did Jeremiah prophesy? That those who forsake God, he says, do not have true baptism. For he says: Heaven was appalled at this and shuddered exceedingly, says the Lord, for this people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of life, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water. And again: She has become to me, he says, like deceitful water that has no faithfulness. And what is written: He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit him? And this in the Psalms: Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head. And again elsewhere: Dying flies destroy the sweetness of the ointment. And elsewhere: For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding. If all these passages are to be understood as these men understand them, the logic of truth does not hold either for us or for them. But if I show that they are to be understood in another way, these men alone are thrown into confusion by their own perversity. To escape that confusion they take refuge in the catholic understanding, and in the very place where they find a way out for their answer, they are caught in the net of the crime of schism. For they themselves certainly have such people. I will not say “they are such,” but I will say what they either admit or most insanely deny: they too have people who forsake God, the fountain of living water, that is, people who live wickedly. For God is forsaken not with the feet but with the heart. They also have the deceitful and faithless, that is, people who profess one thing and live another. They certainly have the dead. The apostle does not allow luxuries even to the more delicate and weaker sex, saying of the widow: But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives. So let them ask whether no men among them, and, what is more, no prelates or ministers, live in luxury. Then, if they dare, let them declare that they have no dead and are better than that church to whose angel, as a figure of its prelates or of its souls, it is said that it does not live but is dead. Yet that church is counted among the seven churches, and it has not been cut off from the fabric of Christ's body but perseveres in unity, and it is even given precepts of life. I pass over what they said in their council against the Maximianists: “Like the Egyptians, the shores are full of the corpses of those perishing.” One of that number of the dead, Felician, is now inside with them, and he still baptizes though dead; or, if he has now come back to life, he has with him those whom he baptized while dead in schism. They certainly have sinners. For if any of those who seem great in their own eyes are questioned, they do not deny that they themselves are sinners. It is not the case that they do not beat their breasts, or that they do so only in pretence, or that they do not say in the Lord's Prayer: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. If they beat their breasts in pretence, then surely at that very moment they sin miserably, deceiving their peoples with feigned humility. That petition is certainly not said about the sins forgiven in the rebirth of baptism. It is said about the sins which the weakness of human life contracts every day from the most bitter waves of the world. The remedies provided to heal these are almsgiving, fasting and prayer, so that in prayer we speak of what is done in almsgiving. For to forgive the sin another has committed against you, so that God may forgive you too, is a great work of mercy. But if they say this in prayer falsely and not truthfully, thinking they have nothing for God to forgive them, that in itself is an inexpiable sacrilege and that very impious and insane pride, which is certainly a monstrous sin. As for the dying flies, what shall I say, since we have shown that among them are found many who are not merely dying but already dead, whether they admit it or are convicted of it? And as for the deceitful, from whom the holy spirit of discipline flees, and those who live in ruin without understanding, let them consider how many they have among them, in light of what has been said above. Wicked people certainly lie hidden there. This is clear from the mere fact that people are often exposed, convicted and condemned, not only for recent deeds but also for an old habit of shameful acts, people who managed to stay hidden for a long time by the most cunning pretence. Whatever wicked people lie hidden there are surely all the more deceitful, since they deceive by pretending to be good.

If, then, these texts are to be understood as these people understand them, how can their reasoning hold up? If this passage is to be understood of the sacrament of baptism, why are those among them who forsake God by living wickedly, whether they are hidden or known, not made into broken cisterns that cannot hold water? Why are their liars and unfaithful members believed to give or to have, not lying water, but true water? Why does washing profit anything to those who are baptized by their dead? Why do their sinners anoint other people's heads with oil? What have the dying or dead flies there done to deserve not to destroy the oil of sweetness? By what privilege are any who are deceitful there protected, that is, those who cover a wolf with the skin of righteousness, so that the holy spirit of discipline does not flee from them? Or if the Holy Spirit flees from them, how is he given through them to those they baptize? For here they cannot say what they usually say, most foolishly and shamelessly: that a person can be baptized by a wicked man if the baptizer's wickedness is hidden. For a deceitful man is all the more deceitful the better he is hidden. Since the Holy Spirit withdraws from such a man, what hope will the baptized person have, if the merit of the human baptizer has to be taken into account in that grace of God? Here they find absolutely nothing to answer, because they deny that they have any open wrongdoers among them. In this, indeed, they are refuted most openly. But what is that to us? For the essential point of the case it is enough for us that they cannot deny having among them pretended good men, that is, hidden wicked men. For they are refuted by many people who lived among them in depraved and criminal ways, lay hidden for a long time by that very pretense, and were at last exposed and expelled. So if they do not want us to believe that there are still some such men there, then certainly those who were thrown out—while they lay hidden there in that same pretense, and the Holy Spirit fled from them, the Spirit of whom it is written, "For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful"—how could they baptize? Why are not at least those of their baptized who are still alive sought out, so that they may receive baptism, which they certainly could not have received from deceitful men whom the Holy Spirit was deserting? But if they say, "The Holy Spirit was indeed absent from the pretenders who gave baptism, so as not to justify them, but he was present to the believers who received it, so as to wash them, by the ineffable efficacy of his power, easily able to do both—to flee the one and cherish the other, to condemn the one and cleanse the other"—then let them see that the question they resolve in their own favor is at the same time resolved in ours.

Now what is to be understood in this sentence of holy Scripture—which they certainly do not understand, and which they thrust at us as if it supported their side, though it serves to refute themselves—we point out should be understood in nearly all such questions: namely, that all the sacraments, while they harm those who handle them unworthily, nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such ministers, just as the word of God does, of which it was said, "Do what they say, but do not do what they do." For what prevents me from understanding "digging broken cisterns that cannot hold water" to mean turning to earthly pleasure and being unable to retain the Holy Spirit, who, as any Christian of whatever kind knows, is signified in the Gospel by the name of water? Likewise, "lying water that has no faithfulness" can be understood not as false baptism but as a lying and unfaithful people—not counting the truthful and faithful, but only those who are liars and unfaithful. For that peoples are sometimes signified by the word "waters," let them read the Apocalypse, and let them stop raising false charges, first and foremost against themselves rather than against us. For thus it is said to John: "The waters you saw, on which that harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues." And as for what is written, "He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit him?"—to postpone for the moment a more careful investigation of these words—I take it with complete safety that the baptisms of the pagans are meant, because they worship men who are dead both to righteousness and to this life, and in their names they baptize. For although their priests too may be called dead through their impiety, the text is not understood in this way because of them, but because of their dead gods, in contrast to whom it is said, "Our God is a living God." Therefore, even if among Christians there are some prelates or ministers who are dead through their iniquity and impiety, yet he lives of whom it was said in the Gospel, "This is he who baptizes," because, as the apostle says, "Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death will no longer have dominion over him." As for "the oil of the sinner," the psalm itself shows most plainly how it is to be understood. For it says: "The righteous man will correct me in mercy and reprove me; but the oil of the sinner will not anoint my head." From this it is clear that the oil of the sinner signifies the flatteries of a sycophant; rejecting and detesting these, the psalmist chooses to be corrected and reproved by the righteous man, because the righteous man, in doing this not with the deceitful gentleness of flattery but with the truthful harshness of rebuke, acts far more mercifully. Hence also that word in the Apocalypse, "Those whom I love I reprove and chasten," and that in Solomon, "Better are the wounds of a friend than the eager kisses of an enemy"; and many such passages are found. As for "the oil of sweetness," that is, the good fragrance spread by the good reputation of Christians, it is destroyed by those who, meaning to live badly and to return to the death of their iniquities, rush in in great multitudes to have their sins forgiven through baptism and then go back to them again. For I think it is because of their great numbers that they are compared to flies. But they destroy the oil of sweetness for those who look not at the grace of God itself but at the behavior of men; and since, just as grains of wheat are not seen among the chaff, so those who live devoutly are not easily noticed among crowds of the wicked, such people take offense in a carnal way and are either delayed in receiving eternal salvation or recoil from it altogether. That a good fragrance consists in the good reputation of Christians who live rightly, the apostle teaches when he says, "We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place." On the other hand, those to whom it is said, "For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you," certainly destroy the oil of sweetness. So these passages have other, sounder interpretations, and if they follow them, they too will be freed from the tight corner of these questions. Their own interpretation, however, if we do not accept it, entangles them alone; but if we accept it, it entangles both us and them.

What need is there to discuss further? Unless perhaps someone will be troubled by the fact that Parmenian, wishing to prove that carnal men cannot beget spiritual children, added a testimony from the Gospel: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." As if we said that any man begets spiritual children by himself, and not through the Gospel, in whose preaching the Holy Spirit works to beget spiritual children in baptism, even when he flees from a deceitful minister, as we learned above. That is why, when the apostle was speaking to such children, if he had said, "I begot you," and had not added, "in Christ Jesus through the Gospel," none of the faithful could with any piety have professed to be born of him. But even Judas the thief preached the Gospel without harm to those who believed; and as for their own deceitful members, that is, hidden wrongdoers, they themselves concede that although the Holy Spirit flees from them, spiritual children are nevertheless begotten through their ministry. For who could bear such madness as this: that while he might call a man who begets children by his wife carnal, he would call an adulterer spiritual? "Far be it from me," he says, "to think that." How then could a hidden adulterer, while he was a prelate among them, propagate spiritual children, if carnal men cannot do this? Or perhaps at that time Christ, or the Holy Spirit, or perhaps an angel baptized through his hands? If, then, a man baptizes when the baptizer is manifestly good, but when the baptizer is secretly wicked, then God or an angel baptizes, and each person is spiritually born to be like the one by whom he is baptized, then let those who desire baptism wish that the men through whom they are baptized be not manifestly good but secretly wicked, so that, with God or an angel baptizing, they may deserve to be reborn in greater holiness. If they mean to avoid this absurdity, let them confess that through whatever man someone is baptized with the baptism of Christ, it is Christ who baptizes, of whom alone it was said, "This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit."

For that passage of the Gospel—"As the Father has sent me, so I send you. When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they will be forgiven, and if you retain anyone's, they will be retained"—would tell against us, so that we would be forced to admit that this is done by men and not through men, if, after saying, "so I send you," he had immediately added, "If you forgive anyone's sins, they will be forgiven, and if you retain anyone's, they will be retained." But since there is inserted, "When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit," and only then is it added that the forgiveness or retention of sins is done through them, it is shown clearly enough that it is not they who do this, but the Holy Spirit through them, just as he says in another place: "For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit who is in you." Now the Holy Spirit is present in a prelate or minister of the Church in such a way that, if he is not deceitful, the Spirit works through him both his reward unto eternal salvation and the regeneration or edification of those who are either consecrated or evangelized through him; but if he is deceitful, then, since it is most truly written, "For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful," the Spirit is indeed absent from his salvation and withdraws from his thoughts, which are without understanding, yet he does not abandon his ministry, through which he works the salvation of others. This is why the apostle says, "For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me"—that is, "it benefits those to whom I dispense it, not me, who am deceitful." For whoever does it unwillingly, for the sake of carnal advantages and pleasures, and would abandon it if he could have these by other means, is certainly deceitful; and therefore the apostle does not say, "If I do it unwillingly, I am of no benefit to those for whom I do it," but only that such a man shuts himself out from the reward of salvation—not those to whom even a wicked servant distributes the Lord's provisions. But since the apostle was not that kind of man, but rather the kind who acted willingly, that is, who dispensed freely given grace with the devotion of a pure heart, the Holy Spirit worked through him his reward as well, which, as he himself says, "the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to him on that day." But as for those who proclaimed the Gospel without purity—who proclaimed nothing other than the truth, that is, Christ, yet not with truth of heart but as a pretext for their own advantage—he allows them to proclaim it and rejoices, certainly not for their sake, but for the sake of those who were being saved through them, holding to the precept of him who said, "Do what they say, but do not do what they do. For they say and do not do." For thus the apostle speaks to the Philippians: "Some indeed," he says, "preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will; some out of love, knowing that I am set for the defense of the Gospel; but others proclaim Christ out of contentiousness, not purely, thinking to stir up affliction for me in my chains. What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice." Would he have permitted them to preach Christ, though they did not preach the truth of the Gospel with the true purity of their hearts—would he have rejoiced at the preaching of such men—unless he knew that it was ruinous to them to proclaim a pure thing impurely, but salutary to those who, hearing good and true things through them, advanced toward salvation? For where it is not Christ, who is the truth, but falsehood and lies that are preached, he forbids it most openly, saying to the Galatians, "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be accursed," and likewise to Timothy: "As I urged you," he says, "to remain in Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might charge certain people not to teach otherwise." But as for those envious, contentious, obstinate, impure men, seeking an occasion to satisfy their own ill will, because the Holy Spirit fled their pretense in such a way as not to abandon their ministry, through which Christ was being preached, he not only permits them to do it but even rejoices that they do it.

We bring forward these proofs from the holy Scriptures so that it may be evident that hardly anything is more grievous than the sacrilege of schism. For there is no just necessity for cutting off unity, since good people tolerate the wicked, who can do them no spiritual harm, precisely so as not to be spiritually separated from the good, when regard for preserving peace restrains or postpones the severity of discipline—a severity which, however, comes into play with confidence when it is evident that something can be punished by the Church's judgment, for wholesome correction, without the wound of schism. For we rather say: "The name of the Lord belongs to those who fear him," even though they are mixed in with crowds of those who do not fear him; and also what the apostle says: "The Lord knows those who are his," and "Let everyone who calls on the name of the Lord depart from iniquity." For if, for the good of peace—lest the wheat be uprooted along with the tares if they are gathered before the time—someone is compelled by necessity to be among the unrighteous, let him nevertheless depart from iniquity, and he calls on the name of the Lord in safety. For at one and the same time he departs from the unrighteous, goes out from them, and is separated from them for the present in heart, so that in the end he may deserve to be separated from such people in body as well.

And as for what is written, "Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner," it is certainly fitting in the mouth of the faithful. Now each person has his own mouth, just as each person has his own burden, and no one is wounded by another's mouth without the consent of his own heart. But when the preaching of God comes from the mouth of a sinner, we must ask what kind of sinner Scripture meant in this passage. For the tax collector, who was justified rather than that Pharisee, was certainly a sinner. For if his sins were not real, his confession of sins was false; but if that confession, for which he even deserved to be justified, was true, then beyond doubt his sins were real. I could say this with perfect truth also of the prayer of holy Daniel, who surely spoke truly when he said, "While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people." In whose mouth, then, is praise not fitting, if not above all in the mouth of the lying and deceitful sinner, from whom the holy spirit of discipline will flee? Yet when such a one speaks the truth, it is not fitting in his mouth, because it is not credited to one who has no share in it; just as prophecy was not fitting in the mouth of Caiaphas, the high priest, who did not know what he was saying, but prophesied because he was high priest. Yet in itself the praise of God is fitting in the ears of those who hear and in the hearts of those who believe.

Indeed, by misusing a sentence of the apostle, Parmenian even dares, as it were, to taunt those whom he denies to have baptism and therefore says cannot give it. "For what do you have," he says, "that you did not receive?" To pass over the context and purpose of the apostle's saying, which the course of the epistle itself makes plain: if he wants this to be understood of baptism, and if the one who does not have it cannot give it, and the one who did not receive it does not have it—so that the text, "For what do you have that you did not receive?" might somehow support him—I ask whether the one who received it among them does not have it. If they say, "He has it," I ask whether he loses it if he leaves them. If they say, "He loses it," then he must be baptized again if he returns, so that what he lost may be restored to him. But if this is not done, and no one says it should be done, then he had not lost it. Further, if he received it and was not deprived of it, he certainly has what he received; and therefore, even on their interpretation, it cannot be said to him, "For what do you have that you did not receive?" Now turn your mind to the very origin of the schism. Whatever they may think of Caecilian, whom we believe to be innocent, he was undoubtedly baptized within the unity, for this division had not yet taken place. Let us suppose, as they would have it, that he himself departed from the unity: he certainly did not lose what he had received. For if he were to return, he would not be baptized again to receive back what he had lost. Further, if he had not been deprived of what he had received, he certainly had it. So not even to him could it be said, on their perverse interpretation, "For what do you have that you did not receive?" Much less can this be said to one who received from the Lord through Caecilian. For why could a man who is not joined to you not receive what he did not have through one who did not lose it when he withdrew from you? How much more shamelessly, then, is it said to the whole world, "For what do you have that you did not receive?"—the world from which the connected chain of this very sacrament came into Africa, and which could not, through the crime of any traditor, lose the promise of God, who said to Abraham in the plainest of pledges, "In your seed all nations will be blessed"—even if these men had been, not impious slanderers of their brothers, but genuine investigators of crimes.

As for what some of them, overcome by the truth, have begun to say—that one who leaves the Church does not lose baptism, yet does lose the right to give it—it is evident in many ways that this is said vainly and to no purpose. First, because no reason is shown why one who cannot lose baptism itself can lose the right to give it. For both are sacraments, and both are given to a man by a certain consecration: the one when he is baptized, the other when he is ordained; and therefore in the Catholic Church neither may be repeated. For whenever even prelates coming from that party have been received for the good of peace, once the error of schism was corrected, even if it seemed necessary that they should exercise the same offices they had exercised, they were not ordained again; but just as their baptism, so their ordination remained intact, because the fault lay in the cutting off, which was corrected by the peace of unity, not in the sacraments, which are the same wherever they are. And when it is judged expedient for the Church that their prelates, on coming into Catholic fellowship, should not exercise their offices there, the sacraments of ordination themselves are nevertheless not taken from them, but remain upon them. And therefore hands are not laid on them before the people, lest injury be done not to the man but to the sacrament itself. And if this is ever done in ignorance, and the act is not stubbornly defended but piously corrected once it is recognized, pardon is easily obtained. For our God is not a God of dissension but of peace; and his Church's sacraments are not hostile in those who have left the Church, but those who have left are themselves the enemies. Just as they have in baptism something that can be given through them, so in ordination they have the right to give it—both, indeed, to their own ruin, as long as they lack the love of unity. But still, it is one thing not to have, another to have to one's ruin, and another to have to one's salvation. What one does not have must be given when it needs to be given; but what one has to one's ruin must, through correction that drives away the ruin, be brought to be had to one's salvation.

And yet, even if a layman, compelled by the need of someone who is dying, has given what he learned how to give when he himself received it, I do not know whether anyone could piously say that it must be repeated. For if it is done with no necessity compelling, it is the usurpation of another's office; but if necessity presses, it is either no fault at all or a pardonable one. But even if it is usurped with no necessity, and given by anyone to anyone, what has been given cannot be said not to have been given, although it may rightly be said to have been given unlawfully. The unlawful usurpation, then, is corrected by a heart that remembers and repents. But if it is not corrected, what was given will remain to the punishment of the usurper—whether of the one who gave unlawfully or of the one who received unlawfully—yet it will not be regarded as not given. Nor will the royal mark be violated in any way by a loyal soldier because private persons have usurped it. For if some people, secretly and irregularly, and not in the public mints, have stamped gold or silver or bronze by striking it, when this is discovered, will not the royal mark, once recognized, be added to the royal treasury, while they are either punished or set free by pardon? Or if someone, whether a deserter or one who has never served at all, marks some private person with the military brand, will not the man so marked, once he is caught, be punished as a deserter—and all the more severely the more clearly he can prove that he never served at all—while the reckless one who marked him is punished along with him, if he betrays him? But if perhaps one who is not a soldier is terrified by that military brand on his body and flees to the emperor's clemency, and, having poured out his plea and obtained pardon, now begins to serve as a soldier, is that brand repeated once the man has been set free and corrected? Is it not rather recognized and approved? Or do the Christian sacraments perhaps adhere less firmly than this bodily mark, when we see that not even apostates lack baptism, since it is not restored to them when they return through repentance, and is therefore judged to have been impossible to lose? Or was it improper to draw a comparison from military service, when the apostle draws comparisons even from athletic contests and proclaims openly, "No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who enlisted him"?

Whether baptism can also be given by those who were never Christians is, of course, another question, and nothing should be rashly asserted about it without the authority of a council great enough for so great a matter. But about those who have been separated from the unity of the Catholic Church there is no longer any question: they both have baptism and can give it, but they have it to their ruin and hand it on to others' ruin, outside the bond of peace. This has already been discussed, considered, examined and settled in the unity of the whole world itself. But if we are wrong, let them explain how the sacrament of the baptized cannot be lost while the sacrament of the ordained can be lost. For they say: 'One who withdraws from the Church does not lose baptism, but he does lose the right to give it.' If both are sacraments, which no one doubts, why is the one not lost and the other lost? Neither sacrament should be wronged. If holy things flee from the wicked, let both flee; if holy things remain inviolate in the wicked, let both remain. If they say, 'Baptism is rightly given only in the true Church,' the answer to them is, 'Baptism is rightly possessed only in the true Church.' Why can it not be given where it is not rightly given, when it can be possessed where it is not rightly possessed? Is it because not having is one thing, and not rightly having another? Then not giving is likewise one thing, and not rightly giving another. Just as one who departs from unity does not rightly have baptism, yet still has it, and therefore it is not given back to him when he returns, so too one who departs from unity does not rightly give it, yet still gives it, and therefore what someone received from him is not repeated when that person comes into unity. They, however, contend that what is not rightly given has not been given. What if someone else were to contend that what is not rightly possessed cannot be possessed? Would we not both protest and say that one who has departed from unity does indeed have it, but does not rightly have it? So if they want him to listen to what we protest together, let them listen to us when we protest that one who departs from unity does indeed give it, but does not rightly give it. Therefore, just as what a returning person had even outside is not given back to him, so what a person coming in had received even outside is not to be repeated. From this it follows that the perversity of men must be corrected, but the holiness of the sacraments must not be violated in any perverse person; for it is clear that it remains undefiled and inviolable in perverse and wicked men, whether they are inside or outside. And when the wicked are said to defile the sacraments, they are said to do so as far as lies in them, while the sacraments themselves remain undefiled. But in the good they remain unto reward, in the wicked unto judgment. For even of the Spirit, who can in no way be quenched, it was nevertheless said: 'Do not quench the Spirit'—that is, as far as lies in you, do not act as though you were trying to quench the Spirit, or as though you thought the Spirit quenched. And the name of God can in no way be defiled, and yet it was said: 'Son and father went in to the same girl, to defile the name of the Lord their God.'

Nor can these men extricate themselves in any way when they are asked why the holiness of the sacrament can be both possessed and given by someone whom God has already condemned as wicked inwardly, and why it should begin to be impossible for him to give it only when he has been condemned by men—although even then he cannot lose it. Finally, why did Felicianus, whom the three hundred and ten condemned along with Maximian, and who was for a long time outside in what they themselves pronounced in their council to be a sacrilegious schism, lose neither baptism itself nor even the right to give it? For he was received back in the very rank in which he had gone out, together with all those whom he had baptized while outside, not one of them being rebaptized. Had they judged that any of those he baptized outside ought to be rebaptized, they would have been judging that he lost the right to give baptism while he was outside; and it would then have followed that they should ordain him again if they baptized those people again. But when they are called back to the peace of Christ, they are slanderers; when they look after the peace of Donatus, they turn a blind eye. What is this but what their own Tyconius said of them: 'Whatever we want is holy'?

Why then does Parmenian exult in empty boasting and say: 'The judgment of the divine law will never allow that a dead man can give life to anyone, a wounded man heal, a blind man enlighten, a naked man clothe, a defiled man cleanse'? It is the Lord who raises the dead, the Lord who heals the wounded, the Lord who enlightens the blind, the Lord who clothes the naked, the Lord who cleanses the defiled. Why does he claim for himself what does not belong to man? Are those among them who do not sin so alive that they can even be said to give life, when they cannot give the growth? 'I planted,' says the Apostle, 'Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth.' How can one who cannot give growth to the living give life to the dead? 'For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.' Are they so healthy among them that they can even heal the unhealthy? What are these men doing but setting themselves up to be blessed in place of the Lord? But they in no way lead astray those who put their hope not in man but in God, and sing: 'Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits, who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases.' If he himself heals all diseases, he leaves none that Parmenian could claim to heal. Are there such great lights among them that they can even enlighten? John the Evangelist does not grant this even to John the Baptist, than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women; he says of him: 'He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light. That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world.' If that light enlightens every man, it leaves no one whom Parmenian could claim to enlighten. For although holy men are in a certain sense called lights, lights that are enlightened are one thing, and the light that enlightens is another; and that light is solely the one of whom the same John the Baptist says: 'We have all received of his fullness.' And who clothes the naked but he who says, 'Bring out the best robe for him,' and of whom it is said, 'This corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality'? Is any man said to clothe another with a divine garment, when it is a great thing if he himself deserves to be clothed? And then, let him dare to say that he cleanses the defiled, if he first dares to say that he is not defiled himself. We have indeed been cleansed by the grace of God. But not even when our cleansing is complete shall we cleanse anyone; how much less now, when the corruptible body weighs down the soul! 'For who will boast that he has a pure heart, or boast that he is clean from sin?' In spiritual matters, to cleanse and to heal amount to the same thing. And just as we have been saved in hope, so we have been cleansed in hope, looking to perfect salvation and perfect purity. How then can we heal and cleanse now, when we will not be able to do so even when we are clean and whole in every way? 'But God,' he says, 'does these things through man.' He does indeed; but he also did them through Judas, whom he sent with the others to preach the gospel, and he did them through the Pharisees in those who themselves did the good things they heard from them, although the Pharisees did not do what they said. Finally, why do the unjust and wicked among them—whether they lie hidden or are tolerated for the sake of Donatus's party—give life, heal, enlighten and cleanse? Are they not themselves dead, wounded, blind, defiled? Or is it that among them the blind leading the blind do not fall together into the pit, because their hearers follow, by hearing and obeying, not these men but the God whom they preach? Just so. But they preach God only when they gather with Christ; when they scatter what they do not gather with him, preaching Donatus rather than God, then the blind following the blind fall together into the pit. But on the question of baptism we shall treat more fully, with the Lord's help, when we reply to all the testimonies of the holy Scriptures that Parmenian thought should be thrown at us—Parmenian, who truly gives his neighbours to drink of the overthrow of iniquity, having served them so evil an error that he not only speaks himself in favour not of peace but of division and rending, but even persuades them that the divine books speak so.

But among many things I am amazed that this man, while arguing that baptism cannot be possessed unless it has been received, nor received without someone giving it, inserted a testimony from the Gospel: 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.' For someone unfamiliar with these words, when he had begun to say, 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him,' might have supposed, before he said 'from heaven', that he was going to say 'by Donatus', or 'by Parmenian', or 'by someone of the party of Donatus', or simply 'by the party of Donatus itself'. I recognize the Gospel, and I confirm that it is written there: 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.' But is Donatus heaven? Is Parmenian heaven? Is the party of Donatus itself? It would not be heaven even if it were in heaven. For he who said, 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven,' would never have said, 'unless it has been given him from the sun, or the moon, or the stars,' though these are in heaven; how much less would he have said, 'unless it has been given him from the party of Donatus,' which not only is not heaven nor in heaven, but does not even want to be in the kingdom of heaven! Nor, without doubt, would he have said, 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from the Church'; for the Church itself receives from heaven. If, however, he had said, 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him by a righteous man,' these brazen men would indeed rush forward and proclaim themselves righteous, so that whoever wished to receive might receive from them. We would not then raise the question whether they were righteous or not; but we would easily show, from certain men who have been exposed and expelled, that there are unrighteous men among them, even if hidden, and that they nevertheless do not reject, nor say was not given or not received, what was given and received by such men. But even this would be said falsely, if it were said, 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him by a righteous man.' For I ask from whom that righteous man, from whom another receives, himself received. If he too received from a righteous man, I ask the same about that one, until I reach, from the very head of the human line, someone who did not receive from a man; and so I would show it to be false that a man can receive nothing unless it has been given him by a man.

What then are these men unwittingly accomplishing through the Gospel testimony, except that people should be reminded at last to wake up and notice that, when a man desires to receive something holy, it is truly not men who must be looked to, but him alone who gives it to man from heaven, since a man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven? If they say, 'He receives it from heaven, indeed, not from man, but nevertheless through man,' I ask: through what kind of man? If only through a righteous one, then those who received it among them through hidden men of the greatest wickedness do not have it. If also through an unrighteous one, what reason is there for rebaptizing anyone? If through an unrighteous one, but only a hidden one, then those whom Optatus, the open henchman of Gildo, baptized do not have it. If also through one openly unrighteous, provided he has not yet been condemned and cast out of the communion of the Church, then those do not have it whom Felicianus of Musti baptized in the schism of Maximian while he was outside their communion—yet no one rebaptizes them now that they have returned with him. Finally, if a man, though receiving from heaven, can nevertheless receive nothing except through a man, I ask through what man John the Baptist himself, who said these words, received what he certainly received from heaven—and none is to be found. And so a bad cause is refuted by the very testimonies it has brought forward. For although the Son says that he received from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit receives from what is his, this is not as though in stages, but as he himself explained when he said, 'Because all that the Father has is mine, therefore I said, He will receive of mine.' Yet that a man can receive something from God with no man coming in between is attested by John himself by his own example, and by so many saints before the Son of God became man; and, after he rose and ascended into heaven, by the hundred and twenty people gathered together, whom the Holy Spirit, coming from heaven, filled with no man on earth laying hands on them; and, once the order of the Church had been established, by the centurion Cornelius, whom Peter himself was amazed to see filled, with those who were with him, by the same Holy Spirit before baptism itself and before the laying on of hands. So no one receives without a giver; but as regards the holiness of baptism, God is present to give it and a man to receive it, whether God gives it by himself, or through an angel, or through a holy man [or through Peter], or through a wicked man, as through so many, hidden or open, whom the servants of the householder are forbidden to gather out of the crop before the time, and whom the Lord's wheat, separated from them meanwhile in heart until the time of winnowing, does not rashly abandon in body like chaff, but bears with spiritually out of devotion.

'One who has believed wrongly,' he says, 'cannot obtain the sacrament of baptism, because it is written: What is crooked cannot be adorned.' What then? Suppose someone among them had been baptized who thought, for example, that Christ began to exist only from the time when he was born of the Virgin Mary according to the flesh, and afterwards, moved by the word of truth, learned that he is the one of whom John says, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,' and of whom he goes on to say, 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' If he confessed to them his former error and anxiously told them that he had held it when he was baptized, would they order him to be baptized again? They would certainly never do so; rather they would rejoice at the man's unschooled simplicity, which had at first been distorted by a carnal opinion but was afterwards corrected by the reasoning of truth. Or if he thought he ought to defend such a perversity stubbornly, and after resisting for a long time without being corrected was even driven out of the Church, and afterwards, having come to know the truth, returned, they would surely judge that he should be healed by penance, not wounded by a repetition of baptism—even though he confessed that he had held this belief in his heart at the very time he was baptized among them. So 'what is crooked cannot be adorned', because the sacrament he had received would not serve him as an ornament if he persisted in a crooked faith, but rather as a punishment; and yet the sacrament itself would remain intact in itself even in the crooked man, whom it did not adorn but judged. And therefore the holiness of that sacrament was in no way to be violated, even while that man's perversity was to be corrected.

Parmenian even dares to set before us divine examples, by which he thinks he shows that a holy man must be sought from whom the sacrament ought to be received. 'The Son of God himself,' he says, 'the Lord Jesus Christ himself, from whom the beginning of spiritual baptism arose, when he was to be baptized according to the will of the Father—is he shown to have come to the faithless and profane Pharisees, or to the most holy John?' But if we are invited by this example to receive baptism, we ought to seek someone inferior to us to baptize us, since the Lord was baptized by one who had said beforehand that he ought to be baptized by the Lord himself, and who testified that he was unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal. Indeed—to set aside a more careful inquiry into why our Saviour himself wished to be baptized—since he wished it for some definite reason, perhaps the reason was this: though he could have baptized himself, he who could even baptize his own baptizer, the Lord wished to be baptized by a servant, and he through whom all things were made wished to be baptized by one who was made among all things, both to teach humility and to show that it makes no difference who is baptized by whom, so long as one is baptized with the baptism with which one ought to be baptized. Nor would he have disdained to be baptized by the Pharisees, if the Pharisees had had baptism of the kind with which he chose to be baptized for the sake of a particular sacrament. For when he was to be circumcised, was John sought out, since this was already customarily done by the Jews? And when the legal sacrifice was to be offered for him, was that temple avoided which he himself calls a den of robbers? Both good and bad certainly entered it, and the bad did no harm to the good, since the Lord, who says, 'Be holy, because I also am holy,' so causes his holy ones to live among the wicked without being violated, provided they guard the holiness they receive—just as the Lord Jesus himself was defiled by no contagion of malice among the Jewish nation, neither when, made under the law, he received those first sacraments along the way of perfect humility, nor when afterwards he lived with his chosen disciples, together with his betrayer, right up to the final kiss. For by the example of him who not only did no evil but also consented to no malice, the grains of wheat are safe among the chaff, because they neither do such things nor consent to those who do them, even if the good tolerate the bad in the same field until the harvest, on the same threshing floor until the winnowing, within the same nets until the separation that is to take place on the shore. But these men are truly blind leaders of the blind: they see so many wicked men among their own number and do not see the way of peace, and they persuade people to follow them not in bearing with one another for the sake of the bond of unity, but in dividing from one another for the sake of the sacrilege of schism.

'But,' they say, 'it was said through the prophet to King Jehoshaphat: O King Jehoshaphat, do you help a sinner, or love one whom the Lord hates? For this reason the wrath of the Lord came upon you.' Which of us says that a sinner should be helped in the very thing in which he wants to sin, as Jehoshaphat helped Ahab himself by going with him into battle when Ahab despised the truthful words of the prophet Micaiah? And yet even so the utterly wicked desert of King Ahab did not harm the innocence of King Jehoshaphat, for the Lord delivered him from the danger of battle when he cried out to him, while he allowed the other, the sacrilegious despiser, to fall into the hands of his enemies. And if Jehoshaphat did experience some danger, which the prophet tells him came from the wrath of the Lord, he deserved it not for another's sin but for his own, because, as he was told, he was helping a sinner. But before God his other good deeds prevailed. For this is what is said to him: 'Have you helped that sinner, and are you a friend to those who hate the Lord? For this, wrath is upon you from the presence of the Lord. Yet good words of God are found with you in all things, because you have removed the groves from the land and have set your heart to seek God.' But one who lives in the Church of God, where there are also those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ, who proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, not sincerely, and who says, 'Whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, yes, and I will rejoice'—such a person remains undefiled and whole among them, because he does not consent with them in seeking their own interests, since he blames and rebukes this; nor does he help them to sin, but helps toward this: that Christ may be preached more widely, and that those who hear and do may, through those who do not do what they say, believe in Christ, hope in Christ, and love Christ. To such people the same Apostle gave this command: 'Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What accord has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God. For he says: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.' Understanding these words carnally, these men have chopped themselves into little pieces through so many divisions within Africa alone. For they do not understand that no one is yoked with unbelievers except one who commits the sins of the pagans or favours those who commit them, nor does anyone become a partner in iniquity except one who either does or approves what is wicked. And who has fellowship with darkness except through the darkness of his own consent, when he abandons Christ and follows Belial? Who casts his lot with unbelievers except one who becomes a partner in their unbelief? For in this way he ceases to be the temple of God, and in no other way does he join himself to idols. But those who are temples of the living God, and who shine like lights in the world in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, holding fast the word of life—nothing that they tolerate for the sake of unity taints them, nor are they constrained, because God dwells and walks in them; and they come out from the midst of the wicked and are separated from them, for the present, in heart, lest perhaps, if they try to do so through the sedition of schism, they should be separated spiritually from the good before they are separated bodily from the wicked.

So it is written that God said, "Those who glorify me I will glorify, and he who despises me shall be despised", and this above all they refuse to look at. For how do they glorify God when they say that his promises could not be fulfilled throughout the world? These are the promises he made to our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, which he announced so long beforehand through the prophets and then carried out through his only Son, who was born for him of the seed of David according to the flesh, so that in him, that is, in the seed of Abraham, all nations might be blessed. They say that the Son of God himself spoke in vain when he said, "Let both grow until the harvest", as if he had been mistaken or had deceived us, since, on their view, only the weeds have grown throughout the world while the wheat has died out everywhere on earth except in the party of Donatus. How do people who think this glorify the Lord, when it is written, "In the breadth of a nation is the glory of the king, but in the dwindling of a people is the ruin of the prince"? Or how do they not despise the Lord? With unbelievable and impious recklessness they exorcize his baptism by breathing on those whose case they never heard and whom they had no way of judging, and so dare to claim for themselves what belongs to God. For the sake of Donatus's peace they take back with their honours intact men whom they themselves had condemned, while against the Lord's peace they curse people they have never heard. They insist that the baptism handed down by the apostles in those parts of the world has perished, yet they grant that the baptism handed out by Felician among the Maximianists has not. Catholics, on the other hand, surely do glorify the Lord. They are confident that no human crimes could prevent his promises from being fulfilled, and they treat his sacraments with such due reverence that they show how, even when unworthy men administer them, those men are condemned for their own wickedness while the sacraments remain in their inviolate holiness.

Again, they say, it is written: "Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things they do in secret." We have already explained how these words should be understood: to take no part means not to consent. For the sake of the Church's discipline that is not enough unless the wrongdoers are also rebuked, so that they can be corrected. But this must be done without breaking the peace, and only as far as the duty of preserving unity allows, so that the wheat is not uprooted along with the weeds.

Again, the same apostle writes to Timothy: "Do not share in other people's sins. Keep yourself pure." In the words that follow he shows how his first statement should be understood. Whoever keeps himself pure does not share in other people's sins. If he shares in them, he consents; if he consents, he is corrupted; and if he is corrupted, he does not keep himself pure. At long last, to be sure, Parmenian woke up and paid attention to what Tyconius was saying, but it did him no good, for at once his love of his own opinion made him shut his eyes against the truth. He says: "Or do other people's sins not pollute others, dearest brother? And is this what it means to have no fellowship with criminals: that even though you associate with them, you do not do what they do?" Yet he has not given the whole of it. It is not enough not to do what they do unless what they do displeases you, and it is not enough for it to displease you unless they are rebuked. Not doing something is one thing; not taking part, that is, not consenting to those who do it, is another; and rebuking them is yet another. So why did he turn away just as he was beginning to see, refuse to follow the matter through to the end, and set down barely a third of the whole? Did he think that he ought to cut off a statement of the truth, just as his party cut itself off from the people? We say that whoever does no evil, does not consent to those who do it, and rebukes those who do it lives among the wicked firm and unharmed, like wheat among the chaff. He says only, "not to do what they do." Still, let us see how he refutes even this third part of the whole statement.

"No one who reveres the law is unaware," he says, "that this is contrary to God's law." So far these are words that anyone can use. Someone else could just as well say, "No one who reveres the law is unaware that this is in keeping with God's law." What is needed is proof, not assertion. So let us watch how he proves it. "What use is it," he says, "to have kept your innocence if you are mixed up with the guilty and implicated with them?" Certainly, if that is so, it is not that having kept one's innocence is useless; rather, innocence has not been kept. For no one can rightly be called mixed up with the guilty and implicated with them except through consent that stains the conscience. But whoever fulfils what is written, "Nothing unjust pleases the just man," cannot be mixed up in wickedness, wherever necessity may force him to live. "Or how," he says, "can you remain uncorrupted if you are joined with the corrupt?" Exactly so, if he is joined with them, that is, if he commits some evil together with them or favours those who commit it. But if he does neither, he is in no way joined with them. Suppose he also adds a third thing and is not slow to punish: the righteous man either reproves and rebukes in mercy, or, if he holds such an office and the need to preserve peace allows it, he rebukes sinners in front of everyone so that the rest may be afraid, and he even removes them from some rank of honour or from communion in the sacraments itself. If he does all this out of love that seeks to correct, not out of hatred that seeks to persecute, then he has fully carried out the duty not only of the purest innocence but also of the most careful strictness. Where the rest is prevented, however, those two things, if always held fast, keep a man uncorrupted and pure: that he neither does evil nor approves of it when it is done.

But let us see what he uses to prove his claim. "Since it is written," he says, "'A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.'" Parmenian said this and passed away, and so he cannot now be shown that in the party of Donatus there is not just a little leaven but a great deal of poison. It came from those asp's eggs that hatched, from serpents now grown full strength, who were condemned on Primian's behalf and then called back again to Primian. "But they have been corrected," they say. Thanks be to God! If that is true, I do not begrudge it, and I wish it might be done completely. For if returning from the Maximianists to the party of Donatus is some degree of correction, how much truer and more complete a correction it is to come back from the party of Donatus itself to Catholic unity! Tyconius, for his part, said many things by which in those times [?], and, as one who knew them from the inside, [showed?] how unwilling they were to admit that their whole lump had been corrupted by their own leaven, and not a little of it but a great deal, they who charged that the whole world had been leavened by the sins of Africans. But if they still choose to understand the apostle's words in this way, I am astonished that they want to defend Optatus the Gildonian so far as to deny that he was even a little leaven. And if they do grant even this much, how big do they think their lump is, that it could not all be corrupted? Or if it was corrupted only in those who approved of Optatus, let them learn from experience to understand what they read: the whole lump consists of those to whom the word "whole" applies, whether for good or for evil. It applies to those who consent; it does not apply at all to those who do not consent. That is why such a thing must be corrected by the Church's discipline, so that it does not reach many others by persuading them. Where the needs of peace allow this to be done and it is not done, the neglect itself incurs guilt, and through laziness in correcting there is a danger of consenting.

By the same rule we should understand the passage he cites next, saying that it is written: "Let it be a perpetual statute for you throughout your generations to distinguish between the holy and the unholy, and between the clean and the unclean." For the further each person advances in the Church, the better he does this. When the blade had sprung up and borne fruit, then the weeds appeared as well. And although the servants of the householder could already tell the two apart and distinguish them, they were nevertheless ordered to let them grow, and to do so until the harvest. But enough on this. What remains needs to be considered and dealt with somewhat more carefully, starting from a fresh beginning.
BOOK THREE

Every devout principle and method of church discipline ought to look above all to the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. The apostle commanded that this unity be kept by bearing with one another, and where it is not kept, the medicine of punishment proves to be not only useless but harmful, and so no longer medicine at all. There are bad sons who act not from hatred of other people's wickedness but from zeal for their own quarrels. They try to drag off whole the weak congregations ensnared by the boast of their name, or at least to divide them. Swollen with pride, mad with obstinacy, treacherous in their slanders and turbulent in their seditions, they hold up the shadow of rigid severity so that it will not be shown that they lack the light of truth. The holy Scriptures command a sharper treatment for correcting the faults of brothers, but with sincere love kept whole and the unity of peace preserved. These men seize on those commands to justify the sacrilege of schism and as an excuse for cutting themselves off, saying: "Look, the apostle says: Remove the evil from yourselves." "Surely," they say, "if this evil did no harm to the sound, it would not be ordered removed."

Meanwhile let us consider whether it was perhaps not without reason that the apostle did not say, "Remove the evil men from your congregation," but rather, "Remove the evil from yourselves." For even when someone is prevented from separating evil men from the congregation of the Church, if he removes the evil from himself he is not mingled with them in heart. In this way he is spiritually not only joined to the good but also separated from the evil. In that passage to Timothy, after saying, "Do not share in other people's sins," the apostle spoke as if it could happen that Timothy would be unable to separate certain evil men from the congregation of the Church and so would be forced to tolerate them. As though giving advice on how not to share in their sins, he said, "Keep yourself pure." For only an evil man can be mingled with the evil. A good man can in no way be mingled with them, even though he lives among them in one congregation. In the same way, here in writing to the Corinthians the apostle first said, "What have I to do with judging those outside? Is it not those inside whom you judge?" Then, so that they would not be troubled if a great number of evil men were so mixed with the wheat that they could not be gathered and separated without harm to the wheat, he said, "Remove the evil from yourselves." If perhaps they could not remove the evil men from their congregation, they could remove the evil from themselves, that is, by not sinning with those men and not consenting to or encouraging their sin. In this way they would live among them wholly blameless and wholly uncorrupted. For it is through his own evil that anyone consents to evil men. If he removes the evil from himself, he has nothing in himself through which to consent to another's evil. Therefore if anyone neglects the discipline of the Church so far that he stops warning, rebuking and reproving the evil men with whom he does not sin and whom he does not encourage, he sins by his own evil and not by another's. This applies even if he holds such an office, and the peace of the Church allows it, that he could also separate them from sharing in the sacraments. In so great a matter, negligence itself is a serious evil. So if he removes the evil from himself, as the apostle warns, he will remove not only the boldness to commit sin or the plague of consenting to it, but also laziness in correcting and negligence in punishing. He must use prudence and obedience in what the Lord commanded, so that the wheat is not harmed. Anyone who tolerates weeds among the wheat with this intention, removing the evil from himself, does not share in their sins. He distinguishes and judges them for now, until the day of harvest, for he does not know what will happen tomorrow. Therefore, with love preserved, whatever necessary severity compels us to punish must be punished, and not without hope of correction. To make this clear enough, let us go back over that whole passage of the apostle's letter more carefully.

"What do you want?" he says. "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?" It is already plain here that he is speaking of punishment, which he signified by naming the rod. Is the rod then without love, since he put it this way: "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love"? No. What follows, "a spirit of gentleness," reminds us that the rod also has love. But the love of severity is one thing and the love of gentleness another. Love is indeed one, but it works differently in different things. "It is actually reported," he says, "that there is fornication among you, and fornication of a kind not found even among the Gentiles: a man has his father's wife." Let us see how he commands them to rage against so monstrous a deed. "And you are puffed up," he says, "and have not rather mourned, so that the man who did this deed might be taken from your midst." Why mourning rather than anger, unless it is because when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it? And he did not say, "mourning because he was being taken away," but "mourning so that he might be taken away." That is, the grief of those mourning should rise to God, and God himself should take from their midst the man who did this deed, in the way he knows best, so that they would not, through human inexperience, uproot the wheat along with him. So when necessity compels such punishment, the humility of those who mourn ought to win the mercy that the pride of the savage drives away. Nor should the salvation of the very man who is taken from the midst of the brothers be neglected. We must act so that such punishment is useful to him, and if he cannot be corrected by rebukes, we must act with vows and prayers. So the apostle goes on to say: "For my part, though absent in body but present in spirit, I have already judged the man who did this as if I were present. When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and my spirit is with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus, you are to hand such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." What then was the apostle doing, except providing for the man's spiritual salvation through the destruction of the flesh? Either by some punishment or even by bodily death, as Ananias and his wife at the feet of the apostle

Peter fell dead, or else through penance, since he had been handed over to Satan, he was to put to death in himself the wicked lust of the flesh. For the apostle himself likewise says, "Put to death your members that are on earth," and among these he also names fornication. And again: "If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live." Yet he does not cut off brotherly love from the man whom he commanded to be cut off from the brotherly congregation. He says this more plainly to the Thessalonians: "If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, mark that man and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother." Let these people listen at last and understand how earnestly apostolic love works to make us bear with one another and strive to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For here too, after saying, "Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother," he at once added, as though showing why he had said it: "Now may the God of peace himself give you peace always in every way." So also concerning the man who had his father's wife, he calls for mourning instead and everywhere commends peaceable love. He says the same of himself: "I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, lewdness and fornication they committed." A little later he says: "I warned before and I warn now, as when I was present the second time, and now while absent, those who sinned before and all the others, that if I come again I will not spare them." So he judged with mourning, so that the mercy of God might crush the sinners and correct them without breaking the bond of peace, in which all salvation consists. We can see that he did this with the very man who had committed fornication with his father's wife. For no one else can be found whom he could mean in the second letter to the same Corinthians, when he says: "Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not to make you sad, but so that you might know the love I have more abundantly for you. If anyone has caused sadness, he has not saddened me, but in part (not to put it too heavily) all of you. For such a man this rebuke by the majority is enough, so that now you should instead forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. So I beg you to confirm your love for him. This is why I wrote, to find out your proof, whether you are obedient in everything. Anyone you forgive, I forgive too. For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be taken over by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs." What could be done or said with more restraint, more care, or more fully with devout concern and with the love of a father and a mother? Just as he applies correction to the sinner, so he wants consolation given back to the man who has been corrected and is contrite and humbles his heart in penance, "so that," he says, "he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow." But what of the words with which he ended this statement? "So that we may not be taken over by Satan," he says, "for we are not ignorant of his designs." For it is Satan who, under the appearance of a supposedly just severity, urges cruel savagery. In his most venomous cunning he seeks nothing else than to corrupt and break the bond of peace and love. As long as that bond is kept among Christians, all his strength to do harm becomes powerless, the traps of his snares are smashed, and his plans for their overthrow vanish.

Even if the apostle was speaking of someone else in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, there too he nonetheless showed how much love should go into the Church's punishment of anyone. This is the very text that these people, failing to understand it, usually treat as the chief of their slanders: "The righteous man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but the oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head." Because they do not know how to correct in mercy, they both hounded the innocent Caecilian with savage suspicions and anointed the power of Optatus the Gildonian with the oil of deceitful flattery. For if, for the sake of the bond of peace, they had put up with Optatus's wickedness with groaning and mourning, they would certainly not be tearing apart the true and catholic peace in the holy unity of the whole world. Or at least they would grieve over that peace, torn apart by their forebears in wicked blindness, so deeply that, having learned at least among themselves how many evil men they are forced to bear for the sake of the peace of Donatus, they would extinguish their forebears' unpeaceful slanders by the peace of their own amendment.

But let us go back to the sequence of that First Epistle to the Corinthians. The apostle had said: "to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." Again and again he urges that this must be done in the humility of those who mourn, not in the pride of those who rage, and he immediately adds: "Your boasting is not good", or, read as a reproachful exclamation, "Your boasting is good!" For that is how some codices, especially the Latin ones, have it, though both readings carry the same meaning. There is no fear that anyone will understand him to have said "Your boasting is good" as praise, since he had also said above, "You are puffed up, and have not rather mourned," and here he immediately adds, "Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?" This can more fittingly be referred to the corruption of empty boasting itself. For pride, as if from the old nature of the first man, who fell through pride, leavens and corrupts the mind, and so swells into one lump those who agree with one another in a like vanity of boasting. To boast, not of one's own sins, but over another's sins, as if by comparison with one's own innocence, seems a little leaven, since to boast even of one's own iniquities is a great deal of leaven; yet even that little corrupts the whole lump. For the proud man falls as his pride deserves, and begins to want to boast even in defending his own sins. Foreseeing this, the same apostle says: "Therefore let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall"; and again: "If a man is overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ." What is the law of Christ but "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another"? What is the law of Christ but "My peace I give you, my peace I leave with you"?
