So what he said here, "Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ," he says in another place: "bearing with one another in love, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." For in that Pharisee too there seemed to be a little leaven, since not only did he not grieve over the sinner, but he exalted himself above the man's sins on the strength of his own merits. But the one who confessed his sins went down justified rather than the Pharisee who boasted of his merits, for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. The apostle therefore goes on to say: "Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened." What does "so that you may be" mean, and what does "as you are" mean, if not that there were some there who were such, and some who were not, whom he was urging by the example of the former to become such? Yet he admonishes them all as one, as though they were the same, so that those who were such would not despair of those who were not yet such and think that they did not belong to the fabric of their own body. For he admonishes them as though they were the same when he says, "so that you may be as you are." Those who already were such knew, and at the apostle's admonition ought to have known better and better, how to bear with those who were not yet such, so that by bearing with one another in love they might keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, and, bearing one another's burdens, might indeed fulfil the law of Christ. And since our Lord Jesus Christ, to teach the way of humility, deigned to humble himself even to death on a cross, and, like a physician with the sick, bore lovingly with sinners, of whom he had said, "It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick," the apostle at once put forward the supreme example, saying: "For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed," so that by the example of such great humility they might learn to purge out the old leaven, that is, whatever pride remained in them from the old man. "Therefore," he says, "let us keep the feast" (not just one day, of course, but the whole of life), "not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." For it is malice and wickedness to boast, as it were, of another's sin, as though each person ought to rejoice in his own righteousness only when he sees that someone else is not righteous. But it is sincerity and truth, even when one is making progress, to remember what one was, and all the more to have pity on the fallen, since one was oneself raised from one's own fall by the mercy of Christ, who, without any sin of his own, humbled himself for sinners.

But lest other people's sins be left to do their harm and be neglected as if by pretending not to see them, which is no less cruel than that pride, he goes on to say: "I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators; not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to go out of this world." That is: if you keep yourselves away from the sinners of this world who are outside the Church, you would have had to go out of this world. For your work in this world is to win sinners to Christ for salvation, and that cannot be done if you shun conversation and company with them. "But now," he says, "I have written to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother if he is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber; with such a one do not even eat. For what have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But those who are outside God will judge. Put away the evil from among yourselves."

See how the apostle arrives at this statement, whose last little part Parmenian thought fit to quote, saying that it is written: "Put away the evil from among yourselves." "Surely," he says, "if it did not harm the good and the upright, it would not be commanded to be put away." But he passed over what was said earlier, leading up to this, although it could certainly have helped him toward what he wanted to persuade us of, namely that separation from the wicked must be made bodily, since the apostle says: "with such a one do not even eat." Why, then, did he not mention what seemed most able to support his purpose? Since he presses so hard to persuade us that bodily separation must be made from those who live wickedly, why does he not bring forward the testimony of the apostle, who says: "If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat"? Surely because he saw that, if he said this, the reply could be made to him: "Is that so? Even if you have no fornicators and idolaters, or do not know of any, do you see and know no one greedy, no slanderer, no drunkard, no robber among you? Why then, against the apostle's command, do you not only eat food at your own table with such people, but even share with them the supper of the Lord's table?" This, as far as I can judge, is what Parmenian tried to avoid: so that this reply would not be made to him, he did not quote the passage that seemed to speak most powerfully for his cause. For if this section of the apostolic letter had escaped him and had not come to mind, he would not have quoted from its last part: "Put away the evil from among yourselves."

But now that we have said this, perhaps they will dare to deny that they have among them anyone greedy, or slanderers, or drunkards, or robbers, and perhaps they will even try to defend Optatus himself, who was notorious throughout all Africa and whom they put up with for so long. Then let them say, if they can, that the church they have now is better and purer than that very unity was in the time of the most blessed Cyprian. He severely rebuked his colleagues, from whom he was nevertheless not separated by any bodily division. He named none of them, but wisely and soberly applied the medicine of a most wholesome sharpness, censuring them in these words: that while brothers in the Church went hungry, they wanted to have silver in abundance, they seized estates by treacherous frauds, and they swelled their gains with multiplying interest. And to show quite openly that he was speaking of those with whom he lived in the communion of one Church, he went on to add: "What do we not deserve to suffer for sins such as these?" He did not say "they deserve" but "we deserve", which he would never have said, since he himself was certainly not such a man, unless he wished to make plain that he was groaning over the deeds of those who were joined to him not only in the unity of the Church but also in the fellowship of the episcopal college, though he differed from them in life, morals, heart and purpose. So let these people say that their church is better now, and that they do not have such colleagues as Cyprian had in that very unity. Let those who wish believe them and shut their eyes to the evils in their conduct that strike the faces of those who pretend not to see. I will call them back to those earlier times of unity themselves and ask them this: when that great man Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage, groaned over so evil a college with the testimony of a free voice, even in writings that would also reach later generations, was the Church of Christ there or was it not? If it was, I ask how Cyprian and others like him fulfilled the apostle's command, "If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat," when they ate the bread of the Lord and drank the cup of the Lord with those greedy robbers, who, while brothers in the Church went hungry, wanted to have silver in abundance, seized estates by treacherous frauds, and swelled their gains with multiplying interest.

Or are these perhaps small crimes, to be thought of as small? For these people tend to say this too, weighing such things not on the fair balance of the divine Scriptures but on the deceitful balance of their own customs. For whatever crime and iniquity intoxicates the multitude loses the truth of the scales. But this is why the oracles of the heavenly pages are set before men like a perfectly clear mirror: so that each may see there how great any sin is, a sin that may in fact be great and yet be made light of through the blind habit of those who live wickedly. Could greed have been more gravely accused by the divine words than by being shown to be equal to idolatry and called by its name, as the apostle says: "and greed, which is idolatry"? Could it have been judged deserving of a greater penalty than by being placed among those crimes whose slaves will not possess the kingdom of God? Let them open the eyes of the heart, so that the eyes of the body are not open in vain, and let them read the free preacher of the truth writing in that same First Epistle to the Corinthians: "Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with men, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God." How then did Cyprian and other wheat of the Lord like him, in that Church of unity at that time, eat the bread of the Lord and drink the cup of the Lord with the greedy and with robbers, with those who will not possess the kingdom of God, and these not laymen or clergy of any sort but bishops themselves, when the same apostle commands us not to associate with them and cries out not even to eat with such people? Or was it that, since they could not be separated from them bodily without uprooting the wheat as well, it was enough for them to be separated from such men in heart and to be distinct in life and conduct, for the sake of the greater good of preserving peace and unity, for the salvation of the weak and of the wheat still, as it were, at the milk stage, so as not to tear the members of the body of Christ by sacrilegious schisms?

But look, I am not pressing any of them to understand it this way. Let them explain for themselves how that Church at that time could have been glorious, without spot or wrinkle, when, while brothers in the Church went hungry, men wanted to have silver in abundance, seized estates by treacherous frauds, swelled their gains with multiplying interest, and were wrapped up in such great iniquities that because of them they would not possess the kingdom of God. But if the glorious Church without spot or wrinkle was reckoned to consist only of those who mourned and groaned over the iniquities committed in their midst, for which reason, according to the prophecy of holy Ezekiel, such people deserved to be marked with a sign of their own, so as to escape in perfect safety from the devastation and destruction of the wicked, then let them stop slandering the good, who do not commit evil out of diseased desire but tolerate it out of peaceable love, those to whom it was said: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God." For this is why the Holy Spirit, through the prophet Ezekiel just mentioned, described the wicked whom the good tolerate in unity with such a phrase as to say that they were placed in the midst of the good. Had he said that the good were in the midst of the wicked, the wicked would have seemed to be outside, on the exterior. "They groan," he says, "and mourn over the iniquities of my people which are committed in their midst," so that we might think of those wicked men as not merely not shut out, but actually shut in.

But suppose there was already no Church at that time, because Cyprian and whoever were with him knew those greedy robbers, such as they themselves were not, and although they accused them with the deepest groans and the most splendid words, they nevertheless attended [?] one church with them and handled the same sacraments in one congregation, and so through communion of this kind came to share the same lot, because they did not obey the apostle, who commands not even to eat with such people, and says: "Put away the evil from among yourselves." If so, why do we labour any further? Why do they boast that they have any church at all, if it had already ceased to exist in those times? Let them tell us where Majorinus or Donatus was born from, so that through them Parmenian and Primian could be born. For what good does it do them to lie now that they either have no greedy men and robbers, with whom the apostle forbids us to eat, in their congregation, or do not know of any, since there were such men in that Church of unity from which they boast that they themselves sprang, and in such a way that they try to persuade us that it survived only in their own society, that is, in the communion of Donatus? For if they say that the Church perishes through communion with such men, why do they not say that it had already perished in Cyprian's time? And so, unable to find where they themselves came from, let them stop saying that the Church survived among them, when they say that it perished entirely in earlier times. But if the Church always has remained, remains and will remain in the good, who are displeased by such things, then let these people at last learn not to understand the apostle's words, "Put away the evil from among yourselves," in such a way that, in trying to gather up the tares through schisms, they uproot the wheat along with them. We argue all this so that those who read or hear it may remember that these people have never been able to prove, whether in those times when the events were very recent or now, when the whole world is bound together in Christian peace in the Catholic Church with a far firmer consciousness of innocence, that Caecilian or the others who held to him in harmony were tares. But we say these things so that each person may remain secure in the unity of the holy Church and not follow the deserters of that unity, lest he perish with them: because even if those men had been tares, they should have been tolerated until the harvest rather than separated by the ruin of schism, with the wheat uprooted.

But someone will say: "How then shall we be able to obey the apostle, who commands: 'with such a one do not even eat'? For if he were commanding only a separation of heart from them, he would not say: 'I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators; not at all meaning the fornicators of this world,' that is, those who were not Christians, of whom he says afterward: 'For what have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But those who are outside God will judge.' Since, then, he is giving a command about a kind of separation that is made not from the wicked who are not Christians but from those who are Christians, whereas separation of heart must be made from all the wicked, and so we must be separated in heart from the wicked who are not Christians too, what remains but to understand that the apostle is commanding us not to mix with certain wicked Christians, of the kinds he specifies, even in the kind of association by which we mix with pagans in the ordinary fellowship of human life? And so in another place he says: 'If one of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions,' but here he says: 'with such a one do not even eat.' He therefore permits us to eat with unbelievers, that is, with those who have not yet believed in Christ, at whose homes he says we should eat what they set before us, and whom God will judge, since they are outside. But with those who are inside, that is, 'if anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber,' he forbids us even to eat. So he is urging that the tares be separated from the wheat before harvest time. And if we refuse to do this, since the Lord forbids it, we are going to tolerate them and persist in separation from them only in will and heart, and so we will even eat with such people, which the apostle forbids."

In this tight corner, as it were, of the question I will say nothing new or unusual, but only what the soundness of the Church observes. When any of the brothers, that is, of the Christians placed inside the fellowship of the Church, is caught in some sin of such a kind that he is judged to deserve anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism, and with that love which the apostle himself enjoins elsewhere, saying: "Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother." For it is done not to uproot but to correct. But if he does not acknowledge his fault or correct himself by repentance, he will go out of his own accord and be cut off from the communion of the Church by his own will. For the Lord himself, when he said to the servants who wanted to gather the tares, "Let both grow until the harvest," first gave the reason, saying: "lest perhaps, when you want to gather the tares, you uproot the wheat along with them." Here he shows clearly enough that when this fear is absent, and there remains complete and certain security about the stability of the wheat, that is, when someone's crime is so well known and appears so detestable to all that he has either no defenders at all or none of a kind through whom a schism could arise, the severity of discipline should not sleep; and in that discipline the correction of wrongdoing is the more effective the more carefully love is preserved. This can be done without damage to peace and unity, and without harm to the wheat, when the multitude of the Church's congregation has no part in the crime that is being anathematized. For then the multitude supports the leader who rebukes rather than the criminal who resists; then it keeps itself, to good purpose, from association with him, so that no one even eats with him, not out of hostile rage but by way of brotherly restraint; then too the man is both struck with fear and healed by shame, when he sees himself anathematized by the whole Church and cannot find a crowd of allies with whom to rejoice in his offence and insult the good.

This is why the apostle himself says: "If any brother is named..." When he says "if any," he seems to mean only that a person can be corrected in this healing way when he sins among people unlike himself, that is, among those whom the plague of similar sins does not corrupt. When he says "is named," he clearly meant us to understand that it is not enough for someone to be such a person; he must also be named, that is, be publicly known, so that the sentence of anathema pronounced against him may seem entirely deserved to everyone. In this way he is corrected without harm to the peace, and he is not struck a fatal blow but cauterized as a cure. That is why the apostle also said of the man he wanted healed by such a remedy: "For such a one this rebuke by the many is enough." A rebuke by the many cannot be healing unless the one rebuked has no multitude on his side. But when the same disease has taken hold of very many, nothing is left to the good but grief and groaning, so that by that sign revealed to the holy Ezekiel they may deserve to escape unharmed from the destruction of those others. For they cry out to him who cannot err: "Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood." Otherwise, wanting to gather the tares, they might uproot the wheat along with them, and instead of cleansing the Lord's crop by their care, they would by their rashness be counted among the refuse themselves. So the same apostle, when he had learned that many were already defiled by unclean lust and fornication, did not repeat his command, in writing to the same Corinthians in his second letter, that they should not eat with such people. They were many, and it could not be said of them: "If any brother is named a fornicator or a greedy man or anything of the kind, do not even eat with such a one." Instead he says: "I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, lust and fornication they practiced." Through his own mourning he threatens that they will be restrained by God's scourge, rather than by that kind of rebuke in which the rest keep away from their company. For he goes on to say: "Look, this is the third time I am coming to you. Every word shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. I warned before, and I warn now, as when I was present the second time, so now while absent, those who sinned before and all the others, that if I come again I will not spare them, since you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me." What else does he mean here by "I will not spare" than what he said above, "and I may mourn"? His mourning would obtain from the Lord a scourge to correct those who, because of their number, could no longer be corrected by the others keeping away from their company and making them ashamed, as must be done if any brother is named for some crime unlike the rest. And truly, when the contagion of sin has overrun a multitude, the stern mercy of divine discipline is needed. For plans of separation are both empty and ruinous, indeed sacrilegious, since they spring from ungodly pride and do more to unsettle the weak who are good than to correct the bold who are wicked. So that most faithful witness to the greed of his colleagues, when he ascribed the evils of tribulation which the Church was then suffering to God's censure and discipline, recalled the very wicked conduct he knew of in certain bishops, who wanted to have money in abundance while their brothers went hungry, who seized estates by treacherous frauds, and who swelled their gains by multiplying interest, and said: "What would we not deserve to suffer for sins of this kind?" Then he brings in testimony from the Psalms, saying: "Since the divine censure long ago warned us and said: 'If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their crimes with the rod and their offenses with scourges. But my mercy I will not scatter away from them.'"

So let a person correct with mercy what he can, and what he cannot, let him bear patiently and groan or mourn over it with love, until either the One above amends and corrects it, or postpones uprooting the tares and winnowing the chaff until the harvest. Yet so that Christians of good hope may live in unity, secure about their own salvation, among the hopeless whom they are unable to correct, let them put away the evil from themselves; that is, let there not be found in them what displeases them in the conduct of others. For when the apostle had said, "What business is it of mine to judge those outside? Is it not those inside whom you judge? God will judge those outside," it is as though they answered: "What are we to do when we are so pressed by a multitude of the wicked that we cannot put our judgment into effect by any restraint?" And he says: "Put away the evil from among yourselves"; that is, "If you cannot put away the evil people from your midst, put away the evil itself from yourselves." But if anyone wishes to understand the words "Put away the evil from among yourselves" to mean that every evil person must be removed from the congregation of the brethren by the rebuke of separation, no one will doubt that it must still be done out of zeal to heal, not out of hatred bent on destroying. And as to what measure should be applied and what times observed, so that the peace of the Church is not violated, a peace in which the wheat above all must be spared lest it be uprooted together with the tares, we have discussed as much as seemed necessary for the present. Whoever reflects on these things carefully and peaceably will neither neglect the strictness of discipline in preserving unity nor break the bond of fellowship by excessive restraint.

For this very thing the apostle says, "not even to eat with such a one": how many good Christians do it with regard to those in their more intimate care! They do not hesitate to separate from the company of those they can, both those whom they sense can be corrected by such a rebuke and those they altogether despair of correcting, so that these do not corrupt others by the contagion of evil talk. And the one who does this well, that is, with humble love and kindly strictness, is the one who presides over his brothers in such a way as to remember that he is their servant, as both the command and the example of the Lord himself require. For then it is done without the arrogance of pride toward men and with the mourning of prayer toward God. But a multitude of the wicked in any order of the Church cannot be shut off and driven out from mingling with the good as easily as an individual can be removed: from the rank of the clergy by the bishop, or from the roll of the poor whom the Church feeds, or from the congregation of the laity itself, whether by the bishop or by a cleric or by any superior who has the authority, so that those who can be given such an order do not even eat with such a one. For in their own homes too, good believers so govern and direct the discipline of their households that they obey the apostle's command there as well, "not even to eat with such a one," when they do this, or order it done, with regard to their children and servants, on seeing them live in such a way that the very love they have for them prompts them to do it. But the crowd of the wicked, when there is opportunity to preach to the people, must be struck with a general reproof, especially if some scourge of the Lord from above has provided an occasion and opening by which it is evident that they are being beaten for their deserts. For then the calamity of the listeners lends humble ears to the word that corrects them, and more easily drives afflicted hearts to the groaning of confession than to the murmurs of resistance. So perhaps the blessed Cyprian would not have said those things about his colleagues at that time unless divine severity from above had been assisting him. For he said them at a time so distressing, so calamitous and so full of grief that they not only did not dare to be angry with him, but felt they could hardly obtain pardon from those who were angry. And yet, even if no calamity of tribulation is pressing, when the opportunity is given, a multitude is usefully rebuked within the multitude; for just as it usually rages when separated, so when reproved within the congregation itself it usually groans. Therefore that command of the apostle must by no means be neglected when it can be carried out without danger of violating the peace, since he himself did not want the wicked person separated from the congregation of the good in any other way; and above all, that other command of his must be kept, that, bearing with one another, we should strive to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Likewise we must obey the Lord in the gospel both where he says, "If he will not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector," and where he forbade the tares to be gathered, lest the wheat be uprooted with them. For both can be kept by those of whom it is said: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God."

But now let us look at the other testimonies Parmenian has put forward. Of all the passages that reveal their sacrilegious swelling pride, in none has he exposed himself more than where he has dared to cite even that text from the prophet Jeremiah, by which he would persuade blind men that the communion of the Donatists is not only the true Church but is already, at this present time, such as the holy Church will be after the final winnowing. I do not know what could be added to such sacrilegious presumption and wicked arrogance. In many places in their discourses they are clearly presuming nothing else, yet sometimes they are embarrassed, when the truth begins to press them, when they are asked whether they do not have sinners among them, or whether they are not sinners themselves. But in this prophetic testimony they have betrayed their ungodly vanity and their extreme perversity most openly. For when the holy Jeremiah wanted to show that, even if the good and the wicked share one fellowship of congregation for a time, the weight of their conduct and the end of their deserts are nevertheless far apart, he said: "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" Parmenian, however, wanting to refute Tyconius, who said that the wicked must for the time being be tolerated by the good within unity for the sake of peace and be separated at the end, at God's last judgment, cited this testimony of Jeremiah. With it, perverse and erring himself, he inflames the perverse and erring to the most turbulent and criminal seditions, so that anyone who, puffed up in his fleshly mind, thinks himself something when he is nothing, and regards himself and those like him as thoroughly cleansed grain, no longer thinks he should join the congregation of the Church, in which those who belong to eternal life must bear with those who belong to eternal fire until the appointed end, as the grain bears with its chaff. No other wind has blown the lightest chaff off Christ's threshing floor before the time of winnowing; no other sacrilegious presumption has created all the schisms that exist anywhere.

"The most holy Jeremiah," he says, "warns us, and separates the fruitless and barren crowds of sinners from the honored harvest of the righteous, saying: 'What has the chaff to do with the wheat?'" O trumpet of fury! O voice of accursed pestilence! Is the human race perhaps so mistaken as not to recognize Parmenian as the winnower? Or does he too give place to Donatus, and boast that he has come to a heap already cleansed by him? For I do not know whether he deigns to acknowledge Majorinus before him. Or were these three like the three prongs of a winnowing fork in the Lord's hand, by which the harvest of the whole world was to be cleansed, and Africa was chosen as the place where the cleansed heap would lie, while the separated chaff covered all the rest of the earth? Where then do such great herds of Circumcellions come from? Where do such great crowds of drunken banquets come from, and the countless debaucheries of women who are unmarried but not uncorrupted? Where does such a crowd of robbers, misers and usurers come from? Where do so many Optatuses come from, each very well known in his own region, wanting just as much but not able to do as much? What is the answer to this? That these things do not exist? Or is this also wheat? Woe to the most shameless denial, if they answer that these things are not found among them; woe to the most criminal perversity, if they answer that these are grain. Finally, why did Primian too dare to winnow once more the heap of cleansed wheat after the trident of such great authority, that is, Majorinus, Donatus and Parmenian, so as to separate the Maximianists from his communion? Did he perhaps throw out grain? What then is he, with his followers, who threw out such things? Or has this grain been so cleansed that its grains do not recognize one another and try to winnow one another by mutual condemnation? Could chaff baptize grain? If it could, why do they say, "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" But if it could not, why is it that when Felician had flown outside among the chaff of the Maximianists, all those he baptized there returned with him to that thoroughly cleansed heap, and they now have them all inside, and do not say to themselves, "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?"

So let them wake up at last and understand how the prophet said, "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" Let them first consider where it is said, if they have any human sense at all. Can it be said in the field, "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" when both are borne on the same root? Can it be said on the threshing floor, where they are threshed together? But certainly in the granary: "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" For the master of the house will come with his winnowing fork in his hand; he will clear his threshing floor and store the grain in the granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. In another comparison, all the wheat is signified by the name of sheep and all the chaff by the name of goats, two kinds of livestock that graze mingled together under one shepherd for the time being. "But the Son of Man," he says, "will come with his angels, and all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will set the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left. And he will say to those at his right: 'Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.' But to those at his left he will say: 'Go into the eternal fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels.'" Then, therefore, the prophecy "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" will be fulfilled, when goats and sheep can no longer share a common pasture. If the good fish could say to the bad fish within that net to which the Lord likened the kingdom of heaven, "Get away from us, or let us get away from you, until all are drawn to the shore and the good are put into vessels by the angels while the bad are thrown away," then the saying "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" could be fulfilled at this time. But those who think their congregation is already cleansed grain have flown off, like pure chaff, from the mingling of grain and chaff; and those who do not see that they still graze with goats under one shepherd have been separated from the Lord's flock by the snares of wolves; and those who do not think they have been gathered together with bad fish are not only bad fish but have also torn the nets of unity. If, then, we are to understand what Jeremiah says, "What has the chaff to do with the wheat?" as being fulfilled already at this time, we can rightly understand it only as meaning that they are indeed in one congregation until, at the end of the winnowing, they are separated bodily as well, but that the wheat's heart is lifted up while the chaff's is turned downward. For the chaff seeks its own interests, not those of Jesus Christ, while the wheat lays up treasure in heaven, and where its treasure is, there its heart is also.

The words of the blessed Isaiah must be understood in the same way, which he, likewise not understanding them, tried to twist to the same erroneous opinion. For what does Isaiah say? "Depart, depart, go out from there and touch nothing unclean. Go out from the midst of her and be separate, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." Must the same things be repeated so often, about how the separation of the heart from the wicked is to take place? For he does not touch the unclean who consents to no one in sin. And he goes out from there, so that his case stands secure before God, if he also does not neglect the discipline of rebuking and reproving, so long as peace is kept safe. For whoever wants to desert openly wicked people bodily, as it were, deserts in spirit the good who lie hidden, whom he is forced to accuse without having tested or known them, while he tries to defend his separation.

But let them answer this: if Felician is clean, why did he go out from their midst? But if he is unclean, why are they now touching the unclean? If he was unclean then, when he was outside, those he baptized there are unclean, because they touched the unclean. Or were they all made clean by returning with him? Can these men, then, make clean those baptized outside, whom they did not baptize in their own communion? Why then do they rebaptize others? Or is it perhaps some special privilege to be condemned by three hundred and ten sitting at Bagai, and is that why anyone who comes to them from the whole world is rebaptized, because the whole world did not earn this privilege of being condemned by the council of Bagai? What then? Those who come to Primian's communion after being baptized by Maximian and his other associates who have not returned: are they rebaptized, or are they spared? If they are rebaptized, the privilege of Bagai is violated, since in that council the baptizers of these people too were condemned. But if they are spared, these men should be asked to meet again at the town of Bagai, and, if that number of three hundred and ten has by now become sacred, to meet in the same number and pronounce a sentence there against the whole world, as they pronounced one against the Maximianists. Then, when they want to rebaptize someone coming from any part of the world, he can defend himself by the same privilege, claiming that he ought to be spared just as anyone baptized by a Maximianist is spared, since now not only the Maximianists but the whole world as well has earned condemnation by the council of Bagai. And then they will free themselves from such great odium; for when they begin no longer to rebaptize those baptized in the Church established throughout all lands, and someone asks them why they no longer do what they used to do, they can answer: "When we used to do that, we had not yet condemned the whole world by the council of Bagai; but now, at their request, we have mercifully granted that we should condemn them by the same kind of council by which we condemned the Maximianists, whose baptism we do not repeat." What great thing is it, what difficulty, to grant all the nations so great a privilege of condemnation? Or is it lawful to repeat the baptism of the whole world but not lawful to repeat the condemnation of the whole world? Here too let them rest easy: we find no council by which they condemned so many nations and provinces. They condemned a few people in Africa, by whom they were defeated in the judgment of the whole world, and afterward they did not dare to condemn the judges before whom they were defeated. For what could have been more shameless, what more insane? Much less could they condemn those settled in the other parts of the world, who chose to believe such ecclesiastical judges rather than the defeated litigants. And yet the baptism of the Maximianists, whom three hundred and ten Donatists condemned at the council of Bagai, is recognized, accepted and admitted, while the baptism of the whole world, through which Christ's inheritance has been displayed just as it was promised, in which they themselves were a few years ago, which they could not condemn by any right and did not condemn even by some perverse council, is rejected, blown upon in exorcism, and repeated. O holy condemnation that the Maximianists earned! O toilsome innocence of the nations, which among these people has lost the name of Christian because it could not find such a place of condemnation!

But if, of those coming from the Maximianists, only those are not rebaptized who return together with their baptizers, like those who returned with Praetextatus and Felician, let them first consider how, of the baptism of the same schism, given equally outside, beyond their communion, they confirm it in some and blow on it in exorcism in others, honor it in part and violate it in part. For where they violate it they become guilty, and where they confirm it they turn out to be witnesses to their own guilt. If they confirmed it afterward in such a way as to stop violating it, this would be called not inconsistency but correction; but since they disapprove in some cases what they approve in others, in the one case they stand accused, and in the other they bear witness against themselves. For I ask: why do you not baptize those whom Felician baptized in the schism of Maximian? Because they received the baptism of Christ, or because they received Felician's? If because it was Felician's, he gave it among the Maximianists as a condemned man, he gave it outside, beyond your communion; that baptism is the same as that of Salvius of Membresa and others like him. But if it is because it was Christ's, then with you Felician at Musti counts for more on behalf of Christ's baptism than Christ himself throughout all lands; with you the man who sits at your side after being condemned by you counts for more on behalf of Christ's baptism than he who sits at the right hand of the Father after being crucified for you. The baptism of Christ is spared in a very few lest Felician be offended, and it is not spared lest Christ himself be blown upon in exorcism among so many thousands of nations.

But the blindness of these men is beyond belief. I simply do not know how anyone could believe that human beings could be so perverse, were it not made plain by the evidence of their own words and deeds that they keep the eyes of their heart so tightly shut. When they cite the testimonies of holy Scripture, they do not look at the deeds of the prophets to see how the words of the prophets are to be understood. Jeremiah said: What has chaff to do with wheat? Did he himself withdraw from the chaff of his own people, against whom he spoke so many great truths? Isaiah said: Depart, depart, go out from there, and touch nothing unclean. Why then did he himself touch the uncleanness of that people, which he rebuked so severely, by sharing one congregation with them? Let them read how much he said against the wicked of his people, and how forcefully and truly, and yet he did not separate himself from them by any bodily division. David said: I have not sat in the assembly of vanity, and I will not go in with evildoers. I have hated the council of the wicked, and I will not sit with the ungodly. Let them read what sort of people he himself put up with among that people in his own day. He paid such honor to the mystical sacrament of anointing that he did not despise it even in Saul, the wickedest of men. Rather, he revered it so much that he could not possibly have revered it more. If we were to set their words against their deeds, would they not answer us: 'Plainly we had no fellowship in heart with such people, nor did we touch the unclean in the way that contact can defile. That is, we withdrew and went out from them by refusing them our consent and the approval of our conscience, because not only did we not do such things, we did not keep silent toward those who did them'? But these seditious and insane men, who look for defenses of their cutting-off in the oracles of the prophets, have nothing left but to use the prophets' own words, in their raving impiety, to condemn the prophets' conduct. Or will they say that in those times the righteous were not allowed to withdraw from a wicked people, but in these times they are? What could be more perverse than to say that the good ought not to have been separated bodily from the wicked at that time, when people were commanded to observe many sacraments bodily, but that bodily separation is necessary now, when those things are observed spiritually?

Woe to the blind who lead and the blind who follow! Are they not afraid, when they say such things, that somewhere in the vast breadth of the world over which the faith and name of Christ have spread, in some region very far from Africa, some righteous people may already have done this before these men separated themselves? In that case these men were still living in the contagion of the uncleanness that those others had fled. If separation of this kind from the wicked must be made, who guarantees them, who assures them, that before they made it, it had never been made somewhere so far away that the Africans knew nothing of it at all, just as the party of Donatus is wholly unknown in the furthest lands of those regions? Perhaps they say that what they did not know could not harm them. In that case, what was done in Africa, of which those lands are ignorant, cannot harm those lands either, even if the crimes these men falsely charge against the Africans were true. But if they say that such a thing could not have escaped their notice had it happened, then let them tell us now how many schisms have arisen in all parts of the world. That is asking too much. Let the Donatists of Carthage, or whoever lives near Carthage, tell us how many factions have arisen within the party of Donatus itself in Africa, throughout Numidia and Mauretania. They ought certainly to know the causes of them all. Otherwise some righteous people in those regions may perhaps have shunned the fellowship and congregation of the wicked and gone out from there, so as not to touch the unclean or go in with evildoers. These men may then have been left behind as chaff some years ago now, in some corner of Numidia or Mauretania, when the grain separated itself, and not know it. What, then, makes them feel secure? Only that they hold it as certain that those who separated themselves from the unity of Donatus' communion, which is spread throughout Africa, could not have been good. For if such people were putting up with some wicked men in their neighborhood whom they could not expose to everyone else, they ought rather to have tolerated them than to divide themselves from so many innocent people whom they could not convince of the sins of others, even if they themselves knew those sins very well. Why then is this same innocence not granted to the whole world, with its great multitude and breadth of nations, wherever the inheritance of Christ extends? Then the world could be certain and secure that those who call themselves good and cut themselves off from the unity of the whole earth show by that very act what sort of people they are. For they seem righteous to themselves and despise others, and so they do not sing the new song, because they are puffed up with the pride of the old man. Indeed, they separate themselves from the communion to which it was said: Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. If they were truly righteous, they would also be humble. And if they were humble, then even if they were putting up with truly wicked people in the congregation of their neighborhood, whom they could not expel from the unity of Christ, they would choose to tolerate them out of the love of Christ. Yet how can they form a just judgment about the very people in their neighborhood whom they accuse of wickedness, when in their rash blindness they bring charges against utterly unknown people set so far away from them? Whether they really know that the fellow citizens or neighbors they accuse are wicked is uncertain to the world. But it is certain to the world that in their rash blindness they separate themselves from people far away whose lives they cannot know. It is also certain to the world that, to the praise of patience, known wicked people are tolerated so that unknown good people may not be condemned. Therefore the world judges with security that those who divide themselves from the world, in whatever part of the world, are not good.

Finally, suppose the prophets warned those who came after them to separate themselves bodily from the chaff before the time of the last winnowing, and by such separation to avoid touching the unclean and not go in with evildoers. Why then did the apostle Paul not do so? Were those who proclaimed Christ not out of truth but out of envy not chaff? Were those who did not preach the gospel purely not unclean? He testifies that they were in the church of that time, and later men also imitated his most excellent love, which bears all things. Is avarice not uncleanness? Cyprian did not touch it with his heart, and yet he lived in perfect peace among avaricious colleagues. He had evidently turned a deaf ear to the words of the psalms, so that he sat in the assembly of vanity and went in with evildoers, did not hate the council of the malicious, and sat with the ungodly! Was there not an assembly of vanity in those who longed to glitter with abundant silver while their brothers in the church went hungry? Were those who seized estates by treacherous frauds not evildoers? Were those who swelled their profits with ever-multiplying interest not most wicked and ungodly? Yet he washed his hands among the innocent and went around the altar of the Lord. He tolerated the guilty precisely so as not to abandon the innocent among whom he washed his hands, because he loved the beauty of the Lord's house, and that beauty was found in the vessels of honor. In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, and some are for honor, others for dishonor. And he cleansed himself from such things, so that he too might be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, ready for every good work. He did not separate himself from the great house because of the vessels for dishonor. Instead, within the unity of that house he rebuked and tolerated those from whom he kept himself clean by not imitating them.

But Parmenian knows how to quote the words of the prophet who says: I have not sat in the assembly of vanity, and I will not go in with evildoers. I have hated the council of the most wicked. I will wash my hands among the innocent and go around your altar, O Lord, to hear the voice of praise and tell of all your wonders. Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the tabernacle of your glory. Do not destroy my soul together with sinners, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are offenses and whose right hand is full of bribes. Parmenian knows how to quote this, but he does not take care to notice how these words can be obeyed without any sacrilege of wicked division. For the beauty of the house and the place of the tabernacle of God's glory are found, as I have said, not in all the vessels, though they are all in one great house, but in those that are for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, always ready for every good work. Whoever among these loves the beauty of God's house and the place of the tabernacle of his glory tolerates the vessels for dishonor. He does not leave the house on their account, lest he himself become not a vessel for dishonor, which is still tolerated in the house, but dung that is thrown out of the house. And because of this temporary gathering with the wicked in one house, he prays, saying: Do not destroy my soul together with sinners, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are offenses and whose right hand is full of bribes. Clearly he is praying that he may not perish together with those among whom love commands him to live. He set the offering of that love first, saying: Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the tabernacle of your glory. That is: because I have loved the beauty of your house, and for the sake of that very love I tolerate the vessels for dishonor, since love bears all things, do not destroy my soul together with them. Do we not hear in these words the voice of those who, as Ezekiel prophesied, groan and mourn over the iniquities of the people committed in their midst? Because they were vessels for honor, they were found worthy to receive their own mark, so that when all the others began to be laid waste and destroyed, God would not destroy their souls with the sinners. But these unhappy men presume that they have been cleansed of any congregation with the wicked, as wheat is cleansed of chaff. By this vanity they have bound themselves in advance, so that they do not dare to rebuke the utterly unjust and shameless crowds in the congregations over which they preside, in order to correct them. If they did, they would be forced to admit that these people are wicked, and someone would say to them: 'Surely you are speaking to purified wheat. Why do you admit by these words that so much chaff is mixed in with it?' And so, because they are not righteous, they do not correct and rebuke in mercy. Instead they anoint with the oil of flattery the heads of those whose heads they themselves wish to be, since they refuse to live under the one Head who is in heaven, in the unity of the body that is spread throughout the whole earth. Rightly, then, it may be said to their congregations: Those who call you happy lead you astray and confuse the paths of your feet.

So whoever does not want to sit in the assembly of vanity should not let himself vanish into the smoke of pride by seeking assemblies of the righteous separated from the unity of the whole world, for he cannot find them. The righteous live throughout the whole city, which cannot be hidden because it is set on a mountain. I mean that mountain of Daniel, into which the stone cut out without hands grew until it filled the whole earth. Throughout this whole city, then, spread over the entire world, the righteous groan and mourn over the iniquities committed in their midst. So he should not look for righteous people set apart, but rather groan in harmony with them while they are temporarily mixed with the wicked. He will not sit in the assembly of vanity, because he will sit where his citizenship lies, and he will hear the apostle saying: Our citizenship is in heaven. There he will not be with evildoers, there he will not put up with the council of the most wicked, there he will not sit with the ungodly. Let him dwell in that hope, so that he may one day be found worthy to reach what he now hopes for. For we have not yet risen as Christ has, nor do we yet sit with him in the heavenly places. And yet, because he has given us such a hope, and through that hope we in a sense already live as citizens there, the apostle says: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. In that life of ours which is hidden with Christ in God, we do not sit in the assembly of vanity, because, as the same apostle says, he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places. But this is in hope, not yet in reality. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. This patience these wretched men have lost. Hurrying to separate themselves from the chaff, as they suppose, before the time, they have shown that they themselves are the lightest chaff, carried off from the threshing floor by the wind. Let us hold fast, then, to what Wisdom says: But whoever listens to me will dwell in hope and will be at rest, without fear of any evil. So let us dwell in hope, thinking not of what we are but of what we shall be. For we are indeed children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When it appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. While we dwell in such a hope, we endure no wicked people, no assemblies of vanity, no evildoers, no unjust, no ungodly, because this dwelling of the mind has no wicked people in it. And yet we do endure them, not in hope but in the reality that is seen, in the catholic congregation spread throughout the whole world. We endure them until iniquity passes away, until the weeds are gathered at harvest time, until the chaff is separated from the grain by the last winnowing fork, until the good fish are sorted on the shore from the bad fish with which they were gathered in the same nets, until at the last the goats are set apart on the left from the sheep with which they have grazed so long in the same pastures under one shepherd.

There is therefore no security of unity except in the church that God's promises have made known. As has been said, it is set on a mountain and cannot be hidden, and so it must be known in every part of the earth. Let us hold this unshaken and firm: no good people can divide themselves from it. That is, no good people, even if they endure wicked people known to them wherever they live, separate themselves on that account from good people far away and unknown to them by the rash sacrilege of schism. In whatever part of the world such things have been done, or are being done, or will be done, the other parts of the world are far away. They do not know whether these things were done or why, and yet they remain in the bond of unity with the whole world. Their firm security lies in this very fact: that no one could have done such a thing except people maddened by swelling pride, or crazed by spiteful envy, or corrupted by worldly advantage, or perverted by carnal fear. All these causes bring it about that good people are defamed with false charges, or false things are rashly believed about good people, or even that wicked people, who do the good no harm when they are tolerated for the sake of the bond of unity, are most perversely shunned and the peace of the good is broken. For then the grain is not spared harassment, as men take upon themselves before the harvest what the angels will do at the harvest.

Since this is so, sacrilegious schisms and impious heresies, whenever they are admonished by some scourge to correct themselves, even dare to count the penalties of their own madness among martyrdoms. Parmenian thinks this too. At the end of his letter he urges Tyconius to remain in the party of Donatus and to endure persecutions, saying that he ought not to join of his own free will those to whom they had not been joined even under the pressure of persecution. He even adduces the testimony of Scripture, which says: "Woe to those who have lost their endurance and have turned aside into crooked ways! And what will they do when the Lord begins to look into them?" As is his habit, he brings forward everything from the divine books against his own side. For who have lost their endurance, if not those who refused to bear with, for the sake of Christ's peace, the men they could not convict of the crimes they charged them with? Later, belatedly reflecting that their own party ought not to be split into many little fragments, they put up with men they themselves knew to be most manifestly sacrilegious, men they had condemned and now received back again, and they did so for the sake of the false peace of Donatus. Let them now at last recognize and correct the impiety of what they did, having learned it at least from what they suffered at the hands of Maximian. But no doubt they are ashamed to be corrected by the plainest reasoning, because they have resisted the emperors' commands, and they fear that once corrected they will seem to have thrown away the sufferings they complain of having endured. As if it were not better to lose those things than to perish! For if refusing to yield to an emperor's command has some shadow, some semblance of fortitude, however false and deceptive, what enticement, even of human praise, is there in contradicting the most evident truth? Why do they shut their eyes and bring forward so many testimonies from the Scriptures? When these are understood and turned against them, they reject them; and even when they are taken in their own sense, they still convict them of their perversity. Is it not written: "Do not contradict the truth in any way"? And whom does one contradict but the truth when one resists even a king who commands something in accordance with the truth? But what a human king threatens or punishes is troublesome only for a time. Not so that King who is also called the Truth, who now too cries out to them through the prophet: "In vain have I struck your children; they did not accept discipline." That is why he now mercifully admonishes them through human authorities, so that at the end he may not have to punish them in such a way that the proud will be unable to boast of their condemnation. Under the punishment of kings, human obstinacy can seek to be praised under the false name of virtue; but to be burned in eternal fires neither will be fortitude nor will be called fortitude. For on that day there will be no one to anoint their head with the oil of flattery, no one, deceived by empty illusion, to dream of crowns for the condemned, crying "Well done, well done!" and swearing by the grey hairs of men who had no sound head, and by the ceremonial shoes of men who did not know the way of peace. These men turn such crowds away from the unity of Christ, eager to convert them to their own name, and meanwhile they dare to compare the temporal punishments of their schism with the sufferings of the martyrs. So the anniversaries of their punishments are celebrated for them by a great gathering of frenzied men. Among them are those who, with no one persecuting them, throw themselves of their own accord over mountain cliffs, ending a bad life with a worse death. On that day there will be no foolish crowds to be told, "We are the righteous, who suffer persecution," and the blind will not be sold a worthless stone for a precious jewel, that is, carnal hardness for spiritual patience. There will be no one to recite at the altars the names of the leaders of their madness, whether at the altars they cut off from the unity of Christ or at those they set up under the name of Christ against the church of Christ. For these are the rewards they want to collect. Wanting to have something to sell, they stir up the severity of the authorities against themselves by their headstrong perversity. And the people they lead astray, who think them righteous because they pay the penalties of their wickedness, do not come to their senses and consider why they suffer what they boast of suffering. How little it would have taken for them to notice that what Parmenian says to Tyconius about enduring persecutions and the glory of endurance is just what all heretics say when royal orders of the same kind are issued to restrain or punish them! It is certainly what Salvius is now saying to his own people of Membressa. The men of Abitina, through whom these people had managed to have him driven out of the church, inflicted such blows and insults on him that they even tied the carcasses of dead dogs to his neck, and in the end danced with him to obscene words and songs. After suffering so much, what sort of speech do we suppose he made to his own people, the wretches he deceived into building another basilica for him? How much must he have said about his own righteousness, for whose sake he deserved to suffer such things, persuading them that he was holy because he had suffered, and that the others were utterly wicked because they had done it? The ancient cruelty of the Etruscan tyrants is recorded, that they bound dead bodies to living ones, but human bodies to human bodies. Whether anyone can recall ever having heard or read of dogs' bodies being bound to human ones, and to the limbs of a bishop at that, I do not know. Everyone knows that bishops are accustomed to restrain frivolous and indecent dancing; who ever remembers men whom bishops had called to their aid dancing with a bishop? Or perhaps Salvius was not a bishop at that time, because his condemnation is read out in the sentence of the Council of Bagai? What then? If he too were afterward reconciled to Primian, as Felician was, who was condemned by the truthful mouth of that same plenary council, as its words are recorded there, would he then be a bishop? Or perhaps he would not be admitted, because the sacrilege of schism can be cleansed from the one it has defiled, as it could be from Felician, whereas a man made unclean by dead dogs hung from his neck cannot be purified? I should like to know what they say to these things, so plain, so public, so recent, they who throw their old slanders at us as though they were our crimes. If any of them thinks I am spreading falsehoods, what great or difficult thing is it for him, if he cares for his soul, to go to Membressa, ask whether these things happened, and defend them if he can? For if he says these things are rightly done to schismatics whom three hundred and ten Donatist bishops have condemned, then let them not grumble when they suffer anything, though they have never suffered anything like this; for we convict them of having made a schism from the unity of Christ on the authority not of three hundred and ten, but of the whole world. But if he says that what Salvius suffered was a light matter, I ask this: if an emperor were to compel some Donatist bishop to dance, and threatened him with beasts and fire if he refused, would he not rather suffer those than consent to that? And once he had suffered, would they not recite his name among the holy martyrs? Salvius, then, with whom others danced, suffered something worse than if he had been burned alive. For if any of them were offered the choice between having others dance with him, without dancing himself, and being burned alive, there is no doubt what they would answer he would choose. But suppose he says that the Primianists obtained nothing more from the proconsul than that Salvius should be driven out of the basilica by the men of Abitina, and that these did of their own accord all the cruel and shameful things they afterward did to him. Then why does he not tell himself that in the same way the Catholics can ask nothing more of the emperors than that these men be shut out of the basilicas they hold under a sacrilegious name, while the emperors of their own accord, preserving their royal power and dignity, punish the sacrilegious far more mildly than the men of Abitina, with no imperial law and no judicial order, punished Salvius of Membressa? Let them consider these things, and first notice what they do, and then what they suffer. Otherwise, closing their eyes to their own deeds and opening them only to their punishments, they will suffer temporal things here in vain, and at God's last judgment they will be punished with eternal torment for this very reason too: that he admonished them through such troubles in vain, in order to amend them. I do not go over old matters, where they deceive whomever they can. I speak briefly, I press present facts on them, I point with my finger: the condemned Maximianists are received back, while unknown nations are accused; the baptism of the Maximianists is accepted, while the baptism of the whole world is blown upon as unclean. Look at the people of Assuras, look at the people of Musti, look at Praetextatus, not long dead, look at Felician, still alive, look at their names, cited in the proconsular records among those condemned by the Council of Bagai. By such recent and present deeds they show clearly enough what they were from the beginning. If they suffer anything for perversities and iniquities of this kind and refuse to be corrected, let them at least not dare to boast.

In three books against the letter of Parmenian, bishop of the Donatists at Carthage and Donatus's successor, a new question is raised and resolved: whether, within the unity of a single communion and the same sacraments, the wicked defile the good. I argue how it is that they do not defile them, for the sake of the Church spread throughout the whole world, which the Donatists slandered and so made their schism.

In the third of these books I discussed how we should take the apostle's words, "Remove the evil from among yourselves." There I said that each person should remove the evil from himself. That is not the right way to understand it. It should rather be understood to mean that the evil man is to be removed from among good men, which is done through the discipline of the Church. The Greek shows this, for there it is written without ambiguity, so that we understand "the evil man" and not "this evil." Even so, I also answered Parmenian on the basis of this sense.
